utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Orie, you were questioning Dr. Gow in cross-examination. Before you begin, Defence Exhibit 1 was marked and, of course, you read from portions of it. Do you wish to offer Defence Exhibit 1 into evidence -- I think you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, Defence Exhibit 1 will be admitted. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, if I may proceed? DR. JAMES GOW, recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to take you back to one of your answers given last Friday. You say that still some elements were co-operating with the Bosnia-Herzegovina government in order to try to calm down the situation; I am now talking about the situation just at the moment where the JNA was not yet withdrawn, but where there were negotiations how to deal with that situation, I am talking about a situation in March/April 1992. You said still some elements were co-operating. Are you aware of a meeting that took place on 26th April between Mr. Itzebegovic and General Adzic and a Mr. Branko Kostic in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall a meeting of that nature -- a meeting which might have been that meeting. I do not recall a specific date of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was General Adzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Adzic had been Chief of Staff of the JNA and at the time of which we are speaking continued, I think, still to be acting Federal Secretary for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Dr. Gow, who is Branko Kostic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko Kostic was the representative of Montenegro to the collective federal presidency of the SFRY, as was, and, according to the memoirs of the Croatian representative, was the man who more or less, for formal purposes, was giving General Kadijevic orders through this period to satisfy General Kadijevic's need to have some kind of formal authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was he vice president of the presidency in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had been vice president of the presidency in Belgrade. At this stage, I think it is very difficult to say that he was probably anything at all -- certainly in terms of the old SFRY structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were they representing, General Adzic and Branko Kostic, the government of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were representing the rump Yugoslav authorities, that is, Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was the subject of that meeting in Skopje to define the role and the eventual withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection is uncertain, but I believe that it might have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any declaration issued at the end of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I am quite confident that a declaration would have been issued after a meeting of that kind, I do not recall the declaration itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was the result of this meeting in Skopje, first of all, that it was the intention of the parties, that means both, I would say the Itzebegovic party and those representing the Belgrade government, the intention for a cease fire and did they agree on the need for a political solution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have absolutely no doubt that statements of that kind were made. Statements of that kind were made throughout the period of the conflict in Croatia and throughout the period of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, before and after that. Whether or not that means that I would attribute the judgment of good faith to them would be a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Gow, to go more a bit in the specific aspects of it, was the need for the end of the blockade of Sarajevo airport also one of the subjects discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall; again I can imagine that it would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was the lift of the blockade of the army barracks also one of the subjects that was discussed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I give the same kind of answer again; I no longer have a specific recollection, but I can well imagine that it would have been. There were still some continuing problems of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are you aware of what Mr. Itzebegovic did just a few days, perhaps one or two days, after this meeting in Skopje as far as accepting the results of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware, Dr. Gow, of the response of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the result of this meeting in Skopje? Is it true that they just ignored the result of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I do not have an accurate recollection, but I would have no surprise to find that neither side ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My question was ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- acted on and implemented ------

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: how the Bosnia-Herzegovina presidency responded, not what the response may have been of the other parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I answered the question already, which was to say both the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the other side, I think, could not be said to have implemented any agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you have told this Trial Chamber, you have told us, that the Bosnian presidency in that period of time sought to achieve some kind of arrangements with the local command of the JNA; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is both true that I told you that and true that the Bosnian presidency and the commander of the 2nd Military District engaged in discussions on possible measures for trying to prevent a conflict and for the institution of joint patrols between the Interior Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you presented this as an initiative of the Bosnia-Herzegovina presidency. Could you please tell us what initiatives were taken from the other side, from the side of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I presented it purely as initiative at the Bosnia and Herzegovina presidency, then I would not wish to have done so. My recollection is that that is not quite what I did; I simply said that the Bosnian government sought, or the presidency and government of Bosnia-Herzegovina sought, to reach an accommodation. I think it should be pointed out, if this is the nature of the question, of course, that General Kukanjac, Commander of the 2nd Military District, also paved the way for a meeting between, not only between himself and President Itzebegovic, but also between President Itzebegovic and Radovan Karadzic -- so the initiative was on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so it was not just the presidency of the Bosnia and Herzegovina government but all sides were seeking to achieve some kind of an arrangement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All sides that -- certainly there were people in the JNA and people in the presidency and government of Bosnia and Herzegovina who came together, at least ostensibly, to seek some kind of arrangement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You have just mentioned the name Kukanjac, Dr. Gow. You have indicated that he also undertook efforts to achieve some kind of arrangement. Could you please tell us what the initiative of Kukanjac exactly was but, first of all, perhaps, who is Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I already indicated that General Milutin Kukanjac was Commander of the 2nd Military District of the JNA in Sarajevo at this time. I am not sure of the initiative to which you make reference. Jointly, President Itzebegovic and General Kukanjac, and I do not have a recollection, even if such information was available at the time, which one of them came up with the idea of joint patrols first, but the outcome of their discussions was the idea that the Interior Ministry in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the JNA would set up joint patrols to try to create calm in some areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from joint patrols, Dr. Gow, was part of the proposals of Kukanjac as well that under certain conditions the army, the JNA army, would be transformed into a legitimate army of the three Bosnian nationalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that that was a specific proposal. Certainly I do not recall that was a specific proposal in a discussion of that kind. Certainly at the time there was some discussion of seeking to make elements of the JNA in Bosnia into the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My recollection was that much of this discussion came from the Bosnian side because it would be in the interest of Bosnia and Herzegovina to try to win over the support of the JNA in this difficult and transitional situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You say that was in the interest of the Bosnian side. Dr. Gow, is it true that the presidency reacted on these talks or proposals -- usually proposals are made in these kinds of talks; I will not concentrate on whether it was proposal, just a part of a meeting -- to the extent that either the JNA to be pulled out completely for the full 100 per cent or to be brought in its entirety under the control of the Bosnia and Herzegovina government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that would be the position of the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So either 100 per cent out or 100 per cent in under armed control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not be certain enough to say 100 per cent in or 100 per cent out, but to say that 100 per cent of those who were in would be under the authorities of the official representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just asked you whether it was correct that JNA to be pulled out for the full 100 per cent or to be brought in its entirety, and that gives us a different picture, but I would like to leave this subject for this moment, Dr. Gow, and -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask a question? I am not clear on what is meant by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the presidency, the authorities. Is there a Prime Minister of that Republic as well as a presidency?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that is my understanding of what it is, but perhaps we can ask the question to Dr. Gow who would know even better the sources because it is my understanding as well, but I am less informed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I made use of the term "authorities", it was as an informal label to apply to both the presidency and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina, as was the case also with the other Yugoslav republics, had a presidency, which in the case of Bosnia was a collective presidency, and it also had a government with a Prime Minister. The presidency was the formal representative, in effect, head of state, and the government was in charge of areas of internal policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But you have called Itzebegovic the President; was he merely the formal head or was he the effective head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it can be said that he was both the formal head and by this stage the effective head. The presidency was the highest element in the structure, and the role of the government was -- the proper name of the governments in the Yugoslav republics and in the SFRY was the Federal Executive Council, and it was more of an executive body than simply a policy making and forming body, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to take you back to Exhibit No. 60, that is, the Security Council resolution 757 . (Handed) You drew our attention, Dr. Gow, to the second page of that resolution, certainly the phrase where it says -- perhaps we can put it on the monitors -- especially the lines, "Deploring the fact that the demands in resolution 752 (1992) have not been complied with, including its demands", and then you draw our attention to the non-withdrawal of the JNA, that is, I think, under No. 4, "... any units that are neither withdrawn nor placed under the authority of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina". So that demand had not been met by that party that was responsible for meeting that demand. Dr. Gow, what was the factual basis of the establishment that these demands had not been met? Do you know what facts were, therefore, made known to the Security Council when they adopted this resolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know what facts were available to the Security Council, although many facts were available generally. If I were asked to do so, I could imagine that the Security Council was aware of those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with you that if there was a factual basis that they should have been aware of these facts, I do agree with you, but could you indicate, since you draw our attention to this specific part of this resolution, whether you expect them to have reliable sources for establishing the factual basis for what is written in this resolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could I ask you to -- I am sorry, I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You said that you are not aware of the factual basis for this resolution, the facts known to the Security Council, but would you generally accept that there would be a reliable basis for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that there would be a reliable basis for that. I would even go further to say that I do not recall that this was the case, but at the time there were reports to the Security Council and to the Secretary-General, and I would suppose that those reports would form part of the deliberations of the Security Council as well as material gathered from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What was the date exactly of adopting the Security Council resolution, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was 30th May -- if I may check?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is what it says on the top. Dr. Gow, are you aware of a report of the Secretary-General of the United Nations with the number S/24049 of 30th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may be aware of such a report, I may indeed have read such a report, but I do not recall the report specifically or its content now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: (Document handed). I have to apologise, first of all, for the fact that this is a telefax copy which is less easily readable, but I see from the top of it that it comes from the Sector Headquarters of Belgrade United Nations, so I hope that it is readable. I am not paying much attention to page 1 where there is a spot which is almost unreadable, just two or three lines. Dr. Gow, is this the report I have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall the exact Security Council document number you gave it, but I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, then this will be marked as Defence Exhibit 2 for identification purposes. Mr. Niemann, you have a copy of that. Is there any objection? The Defence wishes to offer this now into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, is everyone is ready? Dr. Gow, I would like to read to you the introduction of this resolution in order -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Niemann is still reviewing it. Give him a chance to review it and determine whether he has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Defence Exhibit 2 will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to read for you the first part of it, the introduction first, being a report of the Secretary-General and it is a report which says in its introduction: "The present report is submitted to the Security Council pursuant to paragraph 4 of Security Council resolution 752 (1992)". I take it, your Honours, that where it says in the heading that it is "pursuant to paragraph 4 of Security Council resolution 762", that this is a mistake, because there was no resolution on 30th May yet with the number 762, because at that same date 757 was adopted. So I take it that is a mistake. But this is a report submitted to the Security Council pursuant to paragraph 4 of the Security Council resolution 752, in which the Council demanded that, "all units of the Yugoslav People's Army and elements of the Croatian army now in Bosnia and Herzegovina must either be withdrawn, or be subject to the authority of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or be disbanded and disarmed with their weapons placed under effective international monitoring; and requested the Secretary-General to consider without delay what international assistance could be provided in this connection". I just read this in order to put this document in its right context. Dr. Gow, I would like to take you to paragraph 4 on page 2 of this document -- to section 5. I am making a mistake. It says there ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 on page 2. It says: "The bulk of the JNA personnel who were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina were citizens of that Republic and were not, therefore, covered by the Belgrade authorities' decision of May 4th to withdraw JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of them appear to have joined the army of the so-called 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina'. Others have joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is under the political control of the Presidency of that Republic. Others may have joined various irregular forces operating there". Is this a fair statement of the situation given here by the Secretary-General of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not ------

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You have some difficulties with the word "fair", but is this a description of the facts that it is adequate at that time, the description of facts as given by the Secretary-General of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it is not a complete description because it does not indicate that somewhere over 300 tanks, over 800 armoured personnel carriers and over 800 pieces of heavy artillery were left with those people who were part of the JNA structures which continued de facto to be JNA structures in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was sharply in contrast, as I think I indicated in testimony already, to the position in which withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia from non-Serbian parts of Croatia and from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So you say they still had heavy weapons and the withdrawal was not complete and, to that extent, this report, while not stating in paragraph 5 that the withdrawal had not been complete, that the report is not complete either, is that what you -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that the paragraph you have read -- I have not had time to read through the rest of the document -- only indicates a partial picture. At that time around one-fifth of the JNA force in Bosnia and Herzegovina was actually withdrawn because they were citizens of Serbia and Montenegro, but the bulk of the force remained, both people and equipment. So therefore, Belgrade which had taken responsibility for the JNA and which had taken responsibility for withdrawing all equipment in other cases in this case was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I will now take you to paragraph 6 on that same second page of this report. I will read it for you so that it will be easier to comment on it, you having not read it recently: "Those who are not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina are said by the Belgrade authorities to number barely 20 per cent of the total. Most of these are believed to have withdrawn already into Serbia or Montenegro, some of them having been subjected to attack during their withdrawal. Others, however, remain at various garrisons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in Sarajevo (sic). "A further category consists of personnel who have been blockaded in their barracks by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina or hostile irregular forces. These are now mostly in the Sarajevo area, where the latest developments have been as follows". I continue, paragraph 6 under (A): "Some 600 to 1,000 soldiers are blocked in the Marshal Tito Barracks at Sarajevo, with nearly 200 vehicles. Negotiations on the evacuation of these barracks continued until 27th May 1992, when they broke down following a mortar attack which killed some 16 civilians in central Sarajevo. On 30th May 1992, the barracks came under attack from rocket-propelled grenades and flame-throwers fired by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina". I will continue with 6(B), Dr. Gow: "Several hundred JNA personnel from Jusuf Dzonlic Barracks, a logistic base at Sarajevo, and Victor Bubanja Barracks were in the process of withdrawing from Sarajevo during the night of 27th/28th May 1992. The convoy, which was being accompanied by UNPROFOR, was attacked by Serb irregulars opposed to the terms of their withdrawal and by units of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and lost its way. Some elements became separated from the rest. 30 JNA vehicles and their drivers went missing and at least one soldier was killed". I will continue under 6(C): "Several hundred JNA cadets, mainly between 14 and 17 years of age, who were blockaded in Pazaric, some 15 kilometres south of Sarajevo, were evacuated on 29th May". Dr. Gow, does this not give more subtle and more detailed information on what actually was the situation at that time in that region, rather than the mere reporting that the demands for withdrawal had not been met?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before Dr. Gow answers that question, I think when you were reading, Mr. Orie, paragraph 6 -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I was reading paragraph 6 and then it subdivides in A, B and C, all being part of paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When you read it, it actually reads "especially in Serb controlled areas"; I think you read it "especially in Sarajevo". It is just that it may be very important if there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I did not do it on purpose, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sure you did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I missed it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No problem. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, can you answer the question? Do you see, Dr. Gow, in the middle of paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does this more accurately reflect, your question is ------

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: More accurately reflect the situation at least in more detail and giving us more information on what the actual situation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and from that individual piece of information you will note that the discussion of withdrawal, as with many other things, was complex. It would be misleading to be distracted by some elements of detail and to lose sight of the big picture in a situation such as this. You are no doubt aware, as I am sure was the Security Council, that at the time there had been a number of violent incidents throughout the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina; that some of those incidents we have already referred to in testimony involved action of the JNA artillery outside towns acting against communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether Muslim, Croat or, indeed, Serbs were inside sometimes. But in a situation like that, in which there had been at least a month of severe degeneration into a situation of major armed conflict, that whilst the JNA in its efforts to move some of its units out of certain areas in which they were obviously sensitive and vulnerable, which is why they were facing problems trying to get out and, therefore, it was in the interests of the JNA not to try to leave them there to perform a useful role, but to try to get them out to preserve them, that the actions of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, indeed, perhaps of non-official units, whilst not helping contribute to a peaceful situation, might at least be explained in terms of the overall picture of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including, if you were to move down -- I assumed that you were going to read further down to the point where the shelling of Sarajevo by General Mladic, who by this time was Commander of the 2nd Military District, is being discussed, and I think if you consider that this action is taking place against JNA units inside Sarajevo, at the same time as JNA and other Serbian units outside Sarajevo are shelling Sarajevo, it is a very difficult situation, a very complex situation, but one which cannot be understood by reference to any individual piece of information. You may also note as you read down the assumption -- I am not sure on what basis -- of the Secretary-General that General Boskovic, who I believe at this stage was chief or deputy chief of Air force intelligence, if it is the same General Boskovic I am thinking of, had given an instruction to General Mladic which the Secretary-General or UN forces in Bosnia seemed to have been taken seriously, but notes that General Mladic, I think ---

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will come to these parts later, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- there seems to be an assumption that General Mladic at this stage, on 28th/29th May, should still be following instructions from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will come to that part of this report later, Dr. Gow. You say there was a risk of being misled perhaps on details of this information. Do you think that this risk of being misled is greater than just referring to one line in the Security Council resolution where it says, "the demand of withdrawal has not been met", do you not think that would create a greater risk of being misled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not because the one line encapsulates the overall assessment of the Security Council representing the reports of the Secretary-General of other UN agencies in the area and of the agencies of the governments of the Security Council themselves. Whilst it may be incomplete with reference to every little bit of detail, I do not think it is the role of the Security Council resolution to itemise every piece of detail, rather than to express a broad understanding of the situation and to indicate in what ways the Security Council intends to act and address those situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, were the members of the Security Council aware of the information of this report and of this report when they adopted resolution 757?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say for sure if they were aware of either because the report itself clearly indicates that the decision, at least my reading of the report (which has been rather hurried just now) indicates that the decision to impose sanctions had already been taken. I may have been too quick in reading that to see it. Whether the Security Council was aware of the report before they acted, I am not sure. It may well have been the case that they were aware of it, even if the report itself was issued after the action to impose sanctions had been taken, and I am quite sure that they would have been aware of most, if not all, of the information contained in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What makes you believe, since you have just told us that you are not aware of the factual basis on which the Security Council members adopted this resolution, what makes you change your mind now saying that they had at their disposal this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not changed my mind. What I said before was that I did not -- you asked me if I knew the information that they had at their disposal, and I said I did not know that information, but I supposed they would rely on reports of UN agencies, perhaps of Secretary- Generals' reports -- you have indicated that the Secretary-General was preparing a report at the time -- and of the reports of the officers and agencies of their own governments; I have no doubt of other sources of information as well. So, all I said was I suppose they would act on this basis, although I did not know (and I still do not know) the information that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I thought that you said you did not know what information was available to them, at least not in detail, and not whether they used it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, yes, I did not know -- I did not know what -- because I did not know what information was available, also it follows that I did not know what use they made of the information that I do not know that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Gow, what was the reason for first adopting resolution 757 and only afterwards releasing this report of the Secretary-General, because since it refers to resolution 757 in paragraph 1 -- it is not giving the number, but in the last paragraphs it is referring to the adoption of the resolution -- do you know what was the reason for this chronological order, first adopting the resolution and only afterwards releasing the report of the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, but it does not strike me as being terribly unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not understand this last part of your answer, Dr. Gow. Could you please explain what is not unusual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not strike me as being abnormal that there might be a Secretary-General's report released after a decision of the Security Council; the two do not necessarily go in tandem. For example, there was a report of the Secretary-General released on 30th May 1995 assessing the situation of UN peace forces on the territories of former Yugoslavia and assessing its mandate just at the point that I think the international UN position was changing, and immediately after two days of the most significant use of air power by the UN and NATO. Therefore, all I am saying is that whilst, no doubt, the report came out afterwards, I am not sure that you can attribute any particular significance to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is it not more usual, Dr. Gow, that the first the Secretary-General presents its report and the decisions are taken then, when we talk about what is usual in the Security Council. Is it usual that they first take the decision and do not ask for the information on which they might base their decision, or is the usual way the other way round? You did introduce the word "usual", Dr. Gow, I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection was that I said "abnormal" but maybe I said "unusual" as well, usual, unusual; if I did, then what I mean is that not basing the statement on an assessment of the majority of cases but on the understanding that there are occasions on which Security Council and other actions may take place, and on which Secretary-General's reports appear and the two are not necessarily -- the appearance of the Secretary-General's report after action of the Security Council is something which happens and is not necessarily indicative of anything in particular, I would think. The -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite clear to you, Dr. Gow, I did not suggest anything; I just asked you what was the order and I did not ask any other question at that time on whether this was a usual order or an unusual order or a normal order or a not normal order, so my question has been answered as far as this is concerned. Dr. Gow, since I do understand that you do not know the reason for that -- whether it is usual or not is a different question -- did any of your sources, you indicated before, ever tell you that this report was withheld because it might have frustrated the determination of the United States of America to impose sanctions on Serbia? My question is whether any of your sources ever told you that this was the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall if any of my sources ever told me or indicated through writing that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, when we are talking about the JNA, after 19th May, what exactly should we understand the JNA to be after 19th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a very difficult question because on a formal level the JNA itself was being disestablished, although it was recognised that even after the date of 19th May some elements of the JNA, as described, remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina partly because of some of the problems you identified in trying to withdraw certain units. The JNA structures continued to be used after the transformation. So, for example, the 2nd Military District command was moved from Sarajevo to Han Pijesak and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was based around the JNA structure. The command of the 2nd Military District continued, according to what I understand, to maintain its links with Belgrade. You can see in this initial period around two weeks after the formal disestablishment of the JNA, as understood, that there was still an expectation that General Mladic's commander of the 2nd Military District or, by this time, Commander of the Army of the Serbian Republic, which was, in effect, the same thing, was taking orders from Belgrade, but some doubt as to whether or not he was following those orders. I think there would also have been some doubt as to whether -- I think this is reflected in the Secretary-General's report -- some confusion as to whether or not he was following orders, not following orders, or whether there was simply some kind of masking of the real situation going on. I think when the Security Council resolution makes reference to the non-withdrawal of the JNA -- and this may be at the heart of your question -- then what you can understand is that the decision of the Belgrade authorities, not only to leave behind personnel who were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but to leave behind the overwhelming bulk of the armed capability of the JNA, as well as the presence of some elements from Belgrade, is what was taken to constitute the presence of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, let me take you a bit back in the history of the JNA. Was not the JNA already disintegrating in the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA, even before the end of 1991, was disintegrating in the sense that its character as a multi-ethnic armed force in which all the peoples of the territories of the SFRY were represented was being lost. It was not necessarily disintegrating in terms of having a command and control infrastructure, the command and control infrastructure, although elements of it changed with the withdrawal of troops from certain areas in Slovenia and Macedonia and parts or the whole, eventually may be the whole, of Croatia, but that does not alter the fact that the infrastructure which made it an army remained in place and was being used. So to make it clear, the disintegration on one level in losing its multi-ethnic character and losing many of the people in it was the case, but the disintegration in terms of having an infrastructure was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So the infrastructure still perhaps could be used although the JNA as a whole was in a state of disintegration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case and I believe parts of it were being lost by the forces to which I have made reference in testimony so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Who was in late 1991 in command of the JNA, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federal Secretary for Defence at the end of 1991 and, therefore, overall in command of the JNA was General Veljko Kadijevic, to whom I have made reference a number of times in testimony already, and his memoirs have been submitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: When did General Kadijevic retire, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Kadijevic left his post, resigned from his post, at the beginning of January 1992, I believe-- it may be 7th January -- I do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But it was in January ------

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in early January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So it is before the war really started in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the area specifically mentioned in the indictment against Mr. Tadic in the western northern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, far before the war broke out, two or three months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Kadijevic left his post approximately two to three months before major armed hostilities broke out on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but not before the idea of the political project for creating new territories had been discussed, decided upon and begun to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, who was succeeding General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Zivota Panic succeeded General Kadijevic eventually, but for a period Kadijevic's effective deputy, the chief of staff, General Blagoja Adzic, was acting Federal Secretary for Defence. We mentioned Adzic already this morning and you discussed his meeting at Skopje with Itzebegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: When was Adzic removed, do you remember when he was removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection is that Adzic was probably removed in May, May 1992; it might have been a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Gow, when was Mr. Mladic appointed in a new capacity? I do understand, but if I am wrong you will please correct me, that he was the Commander of the Krajina Military District; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Mladic at one stage was Deputy Commander of the Knin corps of the JNA. I am not sure what it would mean to say that he was commander of the Krajina Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am not an expert; if you say it is called the Knin corps, what I, as a matter of fact, would like to ask you is what his position was in the JNA and how his position changed later on. Could you tell us what new position he took in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly in May 1992 he replaced General Milutin Kukanjac (to whom I have made reference already) as Commander of 2nd Military District of the JNA in Sarajevo. Following the formal disestablishment of the JNA, he became commander of the VRS, the Army of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: When was that, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, I do not recall the exact date. I would suppose, to be consistent with the decision to disestablish the JNA formally on 19th May, the 19th May or 20th May would be the appropriate date, but I am not certain about that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will not concentrate on that exact date, whether it was 19th or 18th or 16th, or it might even be 13th, but let us say between 10th and 20th May 1992. By whom was he appointed in his new function after the dissolution or while the JNA being dissolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If by his new function you mean as commander of the VRS ---

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is what I mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- then again that is a very difficult question to answer. I believe there were instructions to General Mladic following the instruction to move the headquarters from Sarajevo to Han Pijesak to convert the headquarters into the general staff of the VRS. So, on one level the instructions would be coming from the JNA command in Belgrade but, of course, on another level it would be appropriate in formal terms for the leader of the Bosnian Serb Republic, Radovan Karadzic, to make the appointment. I am not clear exactly what it is that you want to know, but I would think somewhere between those two points you would have an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think the question related to a date. Let me see if I understand the testimony. General Mladic, according to your testimony, was appointed commander of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo in May 1992, but he also became commander of the VRS in Serbia in May 1992; am I correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Mladic, perhaps in May, perhaps at the end of April -- I do not recall the precise timing -- was appointed to be commander of the 2nd Military District of the JNA based in Sarajevo. The JNA command gave instructions to move 2nd Military District headquarters from Sarajevo to Han Pijesak in Bosnian-Serb controlled territory. The 2nd Military District command at Han Pijesak was then converted formally into the general staff of the army of the Serbian Republic, that is not the Republic of Serbia with Belgrade as its capital, but the Bosnian Serb state entity on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I hope I have made that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, well, you have added something, but in any case, when did he become commander of the VRS in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, my answer was that he did not become commander of anything in Serbia; that he became commander of the army of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So he was not commander of anything in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to take you back to the report of the Secretary-General we just discussed. I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 7 first. I will read it for you. Paragraph 7 on page 3 reads: "It will be apparent from the foregoing" -- these were the parts I quoted before -- "that the issue of the deblocking and safe withdrawal of the remaining JNA troops from their barracks at Bosnia and Herzegovina has become linked to other problems which have caused continuing conflict in that Republic and has in particular been complicated by problems relating to the withdrawal of heavy weapons from those barracks and from Bosnia and Herzegovina. UNPROFOR has received indications that the JNA leadership in Belgrade is willing to leave the bulk of its weapons behind upon withdrawal, but the leadership of the army of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina' is unwilling to permit this". Does this part not clearly indicate, Dr. Gow, that if there was no complete withdrawal, it was mainly because of the opposition by the leadership of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not at all clear that it does indicate that. It makes reference to indications -- and the basis for them is not given but I am sure there was some basis for it -- that JNA command in Belgrade was prepared to leave weapons behind. Quite clearly, it was prepared to leave weapons behind with the newly designated army of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It would not be consistent with earlier behaviour to have made a decision to leave weaponry in barracks which would then come under the control of the Territorial Defence or the government authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Had such a decision been taken, it would still only make reference to small amounts of weaponry relative to the bulk of weaponry which had been left in the hands of the army of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was an agreement, I might point out, in May over Sarajevo when the Territorial Defence forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina had blocked the JNA in the Marshal Tito barracks and on which and in response the JNA had taken the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Itzebegovic, at the airport. Part of the negotiations by General McKenzie, the Sarajevo commander of UNPROFOR at the time, part of the negotiations arranged by General Mckenzie were that the two individuals, the Commander, the Military District Commander, General Kukanjac, and Itzebegovic, would be swapped as individuals, and that the JNA would then later, discussions would be there later for the JNA to withdraw but leave its equipment. But the JNA moved out with its equipment creating an incident which was only settled by the intervention of Itzebegovic who was in the convoy with the UN with Kukanjac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, my question did not involve any suggestion of consistency and behaviour of the parties at that time, but let me ask you another question then on this specific part I have just read to you. You said: "Well, the issue of whether weapons should be left behind or not", as I understand you well, "was the issue of whether they would be in the hands of the army of the new Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or not". I may draw your attention to the last few lines, it says that the "leadership in Belgrade is willing to leave the bulk of its weapons behind upon withdrawal", it also says, "the leadership of army of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is unwilling to permit this'." Am I right when I draw the conclusion that the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would never have opposed against leaving behind major parts of its weapons if it would fall in their own hands? Would it not be logical to say that the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was unwilling to permit the leaving behind of arms because they feared that they might come into the hands of the Bosnia and Herzegovina government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not sure I followed the question; it was rather long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will try to rephrase it then. As far as I read the report of the Secretary-General, the army of the Serbian Republic, at least, the leadership of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were unwilling to permit the JNA to leave behind its weapons upon withdrawal. It sounds totally illogical to me that they would oppose if these weapons that would be left behind by the JNA would fall into their hands; it sounds perfectly logical to me that they opposed because they feared that part of this willingness was that the weapons would come into the hands of the Bosnia and Herzegovina government. Can you follow me in these logical deductions, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I can, but if I can try to understand and if the way I have understood what you say is correct; you are saying that it is logical that the command of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would oppose the withdrawal of JNA weapons if it was going to fall into their hands?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, the leaving behind of the JNA weapons upon withdrawal of the JNA itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, they would oppose the leaving behind of weapons if it was going to fall into their hands; that does not seem logical at all to me, if I have understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the report says that the leadership of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, let us say the new government, that they opposed against leaving behind the arms of the JNA. It is my suggestion that this is only logical if you understand the willingness to leave weapons behind as being the willingness of leaving them behind for the official government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, I think I might have got you. It would be logical, certainly, that if the JNA was prepared to leave some of its weaponry behind in areas which would be under the control of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that those opposed to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina would also be opposed to such a decision. It seems to me that that is not an unreasonable statement to make, but it would still not be consistent with the behaviour of the JNA at any other stage and it would not have made any significant difference in the overall balance of forces. At the time you were talking of a situation in which after the disestablishment of the JNA, there were perhaps around 80,000, perhaps more, members of the army of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina and certain other groups attached from time to time which constituted, which had over 300 main battle tanks, as I have already said, somewhere over 800 armoured personnel carriers and over 800 heavy artillery pieces, at the same time as which the forces of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the kind of paramilitary forces to which you made reference on Friday, comprised something short of that, perhaps up to 60,000, of which most 40,000 could be armed and could be armed only with man portable weaponry, that is, perhaps man portable, shoulder-launched anti-armour weapons. So you are talking about a radically different kind of capability. Even if the JNA had left weaponry behind in barracks, and I actually think in a few cases that might have happened, it might have had to leave without the weaponry, it still did not make much difference to the overall balance of the situation in which the armed conflict was taking place, in which there was an overwhelming abundance of weaponry on one side, thanks to the command of the JNA, and because of the situation and, in a different sense, thanks to the JNA, there was not weaponry on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I will leave paragraph 7 for the time being. I will go to paragraph 8. I will read it for you first. "Uncertainty about who exercised" -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder, he has had the document now for half an hour or so, can he not just look at the document without reading it out? We have all read paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: One of the reasons, your Honour, why I am asking -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If you think it necessary, do so, but it just seems to me to be taking an awful lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware of that. I would not propose if Dr. Gow reads it, but if it takes us then 10 minutes to find out what it exactly says, then it might even save time. But I follow your suggestion and invite Dr. Gow to read paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Or you might, if you wish, put it on the monitor and then everyone can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that is possible, that would be fine so that everyone can read it. Have you read paragraph 8, Dr. Gow? Does this paragraph not indicate that General Mladic was just ignoring what Belgrade wanted in respect of the issues we just discussed, withdrawal, leaving behind weapons, whether or not shelling Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It indicates that there was still an assumption both in the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina and on the part of the UN command that General Mladic would be following instructions issued by Belgrade. It indicates that, as had been the case throughout the conflict in Croatia and was to be the case throughout much of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a formal and open sense, the UN could not express certainty about political control or even military control at certain times, but that was entirely consistent with the example I gave from General Kadijevic's book, saying that "we cannot express things in an open way because that would lead to judgments being made". Of course, many of those judgments were being made, or at least half made, on the basis of events. Therefore, I think the paragraph indicates, first, that there was still an assumption that the command, that instructions would come from Belgrade; secondly, that there may well be consistent with earlier times an intention to try to create a degree of confusion, if not deception, with regard to the judgments of international agents present or international observers in more distant places; and the continuing presence of Belgrade troops rotating in and out throughout the three and a half years of conflict, those troops being paid for by Belgrade seems to me entirely consistent with that perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, am I right in understanding that you say this is still in line with the policy as indicated by General Kadijevic who left already three months before, and it is even true that where the Mladic forces or irregular forces attacked JNA units withdrawing that this was all still part of this master plan how to deal with this situation months after General Kadijevic left his post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given that I do not think a decision of that kind anyway would have been entirely subject to the personality of one individual commander -- of course, I cannot be, I might be wrong about that; sometimes in history particular generals have such a strong personal influence, the moment they are gone everything changes, it is more often the case that generals are part of an organised planning framework that they share broadly common perspectives and that they begin to implement operations in a similar way. This, as I understand it, would also be entirely consistent with the Soviet style of communist military style policy of maskirovanja, the idea of disguising actions for purposes of deception.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not exclude that it might have been the personality of General Mladic that finally created this situation described as doing several things in direct contravention of instructions issued by General Boskovic and the JNA leadership in Belgrade; you do not exclude that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be consistent with my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking whether you exclude that possibility, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I am answering your question, if I may, that it would be consistent with my previous answer to say that I could not exclude that possibility, but the weight of my previous answer also went to indicate that Generals are usually part of an organised corporate structure and, therefore, do not usually exercise undue personal influence, but there have been occasions where that can happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So you say there are ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the weight of my answer is -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- you are telling us that there are other possibilities as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weight of my answer is that Generals usually form part of a corporate structure, but that means -- but also consistent with my first answer is that in absolute, logical, theoretical terms, I do not exclude the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to take you now to paragraph 10 and I would ask you to read it. It is partly on page 3, partly on page 4, certainly the first part, the first sentence. That is just a very short line, your Honours. It does not take much time to read that. It says: "As regards the withdrawal of elements of the Croatian Army now in Bosnia and Herzegovina, information currently available in New York suggests that no such withdrawal has occurred." Is that a reliable description of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would regard it as being a reliable description of the situation, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were any sanctions imposed specifically on Croatia at the time, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that -- the only sanction which was specifically imposed against Croatia was along with the sanctions on the transfer of arms against all the territories of the SFRY which was in September 1991. No further sanctions at this stage or any other stage were applied against the Republic of Croatia. At the time in question, the suggestion was that the forces of the Republic of Croatia were there to assist the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would, therefore, be consistent with the demands of resolution 752. There was some kind of formal defence arrangement between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina agreed and, I believe, signed at the end of May, or maybe in June, when the forces of the Republic of Croatia clearly and overtly took action against the forces of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993. There was considerable discussion of the issue of sanctions being imposed against Croatia, and the United States, in particular, clearly indicated to President Tudjman of Croatia that if Croatian action did not desist, then a sanctions regime would be called for and, presumably, decided upon and implemented against the Republic of Croatia. Of course, the formal statement at the time that the forces of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina were to assist the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was always ambiguous, because there was much discussion of an arrangement between President Milosevic of Serbia and President Tudjman of Croatia; that both of them would seek to annex parts of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the arrangement which was part of the whole situation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the dissolution, in the period of dissolution, of the SFRY. So the position of those Croatian forces was ambiguous and clearly at the same time local Croats, no doubt relying in part on the presence of the Croatian army, were beginning to establish, shall we say, at best autonomous arrangements in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, how did international observers look upon the situation? Did they think that there were still portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the control of the Croatian military units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not clear, did they still think? Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Would they think that a portion -- let me just read it. One moment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The next sentence, I suppose, says that "international ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the observation of international observers on the control of Croatian military army units on military still present at the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. If you asked me a question, I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It says that the international observers do not doubt that portions, etc. etc., as you can read it. Do you think that this is an observation that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think my previous answer clearly indicated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask just one question at this point, Dr. Gow? Where it states, "International observers do not, however, doubt that portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina are under the control of Croatian military units, whether belonging to the local Territorial Defence, to paramilitary groups or to the Croatian army", at that time, and this would have been, the date of the report is May 30th 1992 ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be the period April/May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- April/May 1992, at that time were Croatian military units that are referred to in this sentence there, based on your information and opinion, to support the Bosnians or were they there as aggressors against the Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As was the case with the Serbian side, my own opinion is that there was a degree of ambiguity and deception involved, that there were formal initiatives to indicate that Croatian forces would assist the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these were confirmed by formal arrangements maybe late May, maybe in June, and to some extent in this first phase of the war that could be said to be the case. I think there is little doubt -- I stand to be corrected on this -- among external observers that following from the reported agreement of the two, of the President of Croatia and the President of Serbia, that they would both seek to annex parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the real purpose of the Croatian military in this area was to take control of territory with a view, possibly or probably, to annexing it to the Republic of Croatia at some future stage, as was the intention to annex the Bosnian/Serbian territory to the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What was the day of this report that you have referred to? You said, "following the report of conversations or an agreement between the President of Croatia and the President of Serbia there was an intention to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina", what was the date of that report, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember a precise date; there have been so many reports of the meetings. There was an initial meeting between the President, the two Presidents, at a former residence of Tito, the old SFRY President, at Karadjordjevo, at which reports indicate that this was discussed. I think this was in the spring of 1990 or, sorry, maybe the spring of 1991, but I am not clear about the date. Certainly after that there were a series of other meetings between representatives of the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs which took place, among other places, in Graz in Austria. If your Honour wishes, I can provide some detail about this at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is enough. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you were just referring to the Graz agreement, Graz in Austria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to view some parts and some other parts of video clips as well, but I do not know whether it is wise to start with that. I am a little bit reluctant to ask you to adjourn or to make a break two minutes earlier than scheduled but -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: After Friday, two minutes is acceptable, that is for sure. That is better than an hour and a half. We will stand in recess, please, for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I may proceed, your Honours. Dr. Gow, I would like to show the video clip to you that is also taken from the programme Death of Yugoslavia, and it deals with part 5 of Exhibit 31. I will show it to you again. I think it is a bit more than the part shown to you as part 5 of Exhibit 31. It is in the tape that we have given to the Registry. It is scene No. 4, your Honours. I would like to tender that. We have presented a tape with four scenes. I only use three of them. I will indicate that it is clearly indicate on the tape where scene four starts, where scene one starts, so there is a division between these different scenes, indicating the number I am referring to now. So I would like this video tape, scene 4 of the tape, be presented to the Registry, show it to Dr. Gow, and I will ask now and then to stop it to put questions to Dr. Gow on this scene. The first scene, just a rough indication, is the speech of Mr. Karadzic made in the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, have you shown to the Prosecutor part 5, scene 4? I am sure they have seen it since they have offered a portion of that same film, five-part film.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are familiar with the whole tape, and I assume that we are being shown a part of the tape which we did not display. I have not specifically seen the part they are about to show, but we have seen the whole tape.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But you have no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This I suppose will be Defence 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That will be Defence Exhibit 3, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine, Defence 3 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So that is scene 4 of the video clip we have presented.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to show it on the screen, so that I can ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have you communicated with the gentlemen in the booth, they know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They even know by now that we are starting with four and not with one, so we are prepared for it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. You may show it then. (The video clip was shown).

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to start your Honour a bit back, if possible. Yes a bit forward now again. I will try to stay "stop" at the right place. I would like to stop here, your Honour. Dr. Gow, could you please tell us who is the gentleman sitting right in the front of that room so where Mr. Itzebegovic is walking behind him? Could you tell us who this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid that I cannot identify clearly. It looks as though it might be Bogic Bogicevic who was a representative to the SFRY presidency, but I do not see clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to avoid any other loss of time, it is the assumption of the Defence as well, your Honours, that this is Mr. Boljkovac. Could we then, please, continue a tiny little bit and stop again with the next person sitting in front. Could you tell us, Dr. Gow, who is the lady sitting, seen from this point of view to the left of him, but actually sitting on the right of the first person I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Mrs. Biljana Plasvic, one of the Serbian representatives of the collective presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we then move on a bit further. May I ask you, Dr. Gow, who is sitting next to her? The question might not surprise you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I do not see clearly, but from the appearance I assume that it would be Professor Nikola Koljevic, again one of the Serbian representatives to the collective presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. I would like to look at the rest of the video without interruption from now on, your Honour. (The video clip continued). That is the end of this first scene, your Honour. Dr. Gow, are you aware of any other words spoken at that occasion following the words that have been indicated on the screen by Mr. Karadzic? So, what did he say next to what has been shown to us in this video clip and that is not on the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, what did Mr. Karadzic say next?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic said next.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall what Mr. Karadzic said next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything he said just before this part of the -- are you aware of the content of the rest of his speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been aware of the speech and its content, but I am not sure that I recall, I would be able to recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: OK. I come to that later Dr. Gow. I first would like to concentrate on the date of this meeting of the Parliament. You were in some doubt when you said in your testimony that as far as you remember it was March '92. Perhaps reconsidering the pictures and having seen them again, could you be more precise on whether this was a mistake that it was in March '92 or that you know another date on which this event took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, there was a degree of uncertainty in my mind at the time I was giving evidence. It is not always easy instantly to recall things perfectly in this situation which is not one of the easiest in the world. That uncertainty I think, I was justified in expressing that uncertainty because my understanding is that that statement was actually probably made earlier than that in the autumn of 1991. At the time, and I express this again with a degree of uncertainty, but on reflection that it may make more sense in trying to situate the context of everything, in October'ish, around the time in the autumn of 1991, at the time of the discussions on the statement of sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but again I say that expressing a degree of caution because sometimes it is not possible in a situation like this to recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well if you say now that it is more probable, I note you are making some reservations that it is more probable that it is the autumn of 1991 when the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina was discussed in parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be fair, it would be fair to say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be of any help if I draw your attention to the presence of certain persons sitting in front? Would that be of any help in being more certain about a period of time, especially all these Serb representatives were sitting there? Were they still in parliament in 1992, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I find it difficult to make a precise recollection of that. The Serbian delegates after, I think after November but again this part of events and the chronology, the internal politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is less central to my particular field of expertise, but my recollection is that they began to boycott the parliament, although both Mrs. Plasvic and Dr. Koljevic remained members of the collective presidency, and I think I already indicated that at the time of incident in Bijelina Mrs. Plasvic was part of the collective presidential delegation which was sent there ostensibly to investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you think, Dr. Gow, that it is of any relevance to whether you situate this meeting and the words spoken either in a discussion on the right of self-determination of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or that we situate it in the context of a war to break out within one month afterwards? Do you think it is of any relevance, do you think the difference is relevant as to whether these words have been spoken let us say in October 1991 or in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure. It is possible that there might be some relevance, although I think the essence would be, the essence of the words being spoken would remain the same, because whether in the context of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether this was a statement, in effect a threat, being made in October or in March, the content would remain the same and the overall situation would remain the same, that is a dispute, a political dispute, between one element, the government and the Muslim party and the Croat party in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the main Serbian party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that dispute was the same dispute in October and in March; and at the same time the statement in October, if I am right in supposing that it was October, that if I am right in supposing that that statement was in October, then it would also be subsequent to the declaration of Serbian autonomous regions in four locations or four areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, therefore, consistent with the programme of action to create Serbian controlled areas which would not be part of Bosnia and Herzegovina unless Bosnia and Herzegovina agreed to remain part of a new federal Yugoslavia which would be de facto Serbian dominated and which the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina had already indicated he would not be prepared to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well, Dr. Gow, that the words are the same and the meaning of the words might be the same, but the different context might be relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I find it -- I do not see that there would be any particular relevance in the words being expressed in a difference in time because they are pertinent to the same political dispute, but again not being in a position to say that I can imagine all possibilities, then it may be that there is some relevance which escapes me, but I think the essence of the problem remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You do not think it is relevant that the words when spoken in October 1991 would be part of a discussion on the self-determination while in March/April the situation was totally different, independence being declared already, you are dealing with a state that considered itself to be a sovereign state by then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was always sustained as a sovereign state. The platform on sovereignty reasserted or reaffirmed the formal sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. That formal reaffirmation of sovereignty followed the declaration of the four Serbian autonomous regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The suggestion that -- the only significance that I possibly could attach, now I think about it, to the different time periods is the fact that Mr. Karadzic was uttering these words in October might -- I stress "might" -- be taken as a justification for whatever limited measures others in Bosnia and Herzegovina were to begin to take to protect themselves through the use of armed force, although those were extremely limited. But the suggestion of President Karadzic that the Muslim people, that this action could end up resulting in the non-existence of the Muslim people -- the word is "nestanak", non-existence -- then I think there might be significance in that sense and a significance which would be slightly different if it were at a later stage when the situation were more developed. But I think I would still go back to my original response, that there is no real major difference between the two situations but, I say again, with the caveat that again I may miss the significant difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: OK. Dr. Gow, let us then concentrate on the words of Mr. Karadzic. Are you aware of the existence of an organisation that is called the FBIS, the Foreign Broadcast Information Service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to this Trial Chamber what the task of this organisation is, where it is based, tell the Trial Chamber what you know about the FBIS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the Foreign Broadcast Information Service which has attached to it a joint publications research service. It is an agency working for the United States government, I believe, based in Virginia, which uses information gathered through international monitoring, particularly in the UK Caversham and Cheltenham monitoring centres, monitor the FBIS, in particular monitors radio and television transmissions in certain areas of the world organised in certain designated regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you regard the FBIS generally as a reliable source of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
