utterances.text: Given that the FBIS, as with the BBC SWB, which I think has already been discussed, monitors broadcasts and, therefore, reproduces in translation what is broadcast, yes, it is, because apart from any editorial decision as to which extracts to put into the published version of the FBIS or the SWB, it is simply reporting things that were said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you please have a look at this document? (Handed). Again, your Honours, I have to apologise for the bad quality of it but we received it by telefax. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, do you recognise this document as a document that looks as if it comes from the FBIS? I do understand that you cannot confirm this for sure, but is this the kind of documents the FBIS -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would see absolutely no reason to doubt that this was taken from the FBIS Eastern Europe edition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you, as far as possible with this bad text, read the part especially the right side, the right column, of this page, would you please read if carefully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid it would take a great deal of care to read it. I find it very difficult to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will try to draw your attention to the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have any objection to this exhibit being offered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I gather it will be Defence 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 4 will be admitted. My colleague has suggested that perhaps if it is put on the screen, the overhead projector, we will have better luck with being able to decipher its print here. MR. ORIE (To the witness): I would like to draw your attention to exactly that part that is on the screen now, Dr. Gow. I will read it just to be sure that our understanding of what it says is -- a little bit more to the left perhaps. That is fine. So I start reading after where it says, "Boots and whistles". It then continues : "Let there be great words. Great situations demand great words. How will you prevent everyone from being killed in Bosnia?" Dr. Gow, would not this additional text spoken by Mr. Karadzic change considerably what he said before, even if he expressed a threat against Muslims, does he not say that the problem is how to prevent every one from being killed, not paying attention whether they are Muslims, Croats, Serbs or whoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is certainly the case that those words appear on the screen, the words that you quoted; there may be, and they would add some qualification to the statement that was put before. In the context, I am not certain the degree of qualification that they would add, and I am not sure how you would come to judge that qualification. The essence of the situation, I think I should point out again, was one in which Serbian autonomous regions had been declared in September and, indeed -- something which I have not mentioned before, I do not believe -- in April certain, prior to the declarations of autonomous regions, associations and municipalities had been declared as well. At the time of the declaration of those associations and municipalities in April, they were already felt by some in Bosnia and Herzegovina to be clear indications of the situation in which the Muslim population would find itself later. For example, and I admit that this would only be an indication of the character, the assessment of the character of a situation by one individual but, for example, I think, in the Bosnian newspaper, Bosanski Pogledi, in April -- I think it was 18th April -- at the time these associations of municipalities were being declared, whatever was going on at the time certainly led the cartoonist on that newspaper to draw a cartoon which indicated a street scene I think in Banja Luka in which the Muslims would be walking around with arm bands and wearing crescent and star arm bands in a reference, obviously, to the situation of the Jews in Nazi Germany. As I say, it is an indication from one cartoon at the time certain things were taking place. It cannot tell you everything, but sometimes something like that gives you a little bit more a message than other things. Therefore, the threat of non-existence for the Muslim people might be seen in that context and the context which would, whatever the qualification provided by the quotation you read, would not -- I do not think that -- sorry, whatever that qualification is, I do not think it would significantly diminish the sense that that was the situation which was emerging on those territories, and one which, I think, was to see some greater manifestation in the months and years to come. I might also point out, that newspaper to which I made reference was owned by a man called Adil Zvlfikarpasic who was a Muslim who had been part of the Party of Democratic Action. Initially, had been -- he was a businessman in Switzerland who had provided a lot of the funding, but by this time was entering into negotiations with the Serbian communities and with Belgrade trying to see if there were other ways in which this situation might be resolved. Forgive me, it is a long answer to what was ostensibly a very simple question, but I think it is very difficult to take one line as a significant qualification of the statement made before when there is a broader context, but I meant that that one moment in itself only gives again one partial reflection of the developing situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, the only thing, as a matter of fact, was asking you but perhaps I will rephrase -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered "yes" to a degree. That is about what it comes to, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I will not go into further detail as far as the text and meaning of it is concerned. (To the witness): The only question I would like to ask, Dr. Gow, were you involved in making the selection for that film of those parts that really came into it? You said that you were a consultant in the -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indeed said that I was one of the consultants involved at various stages in the making of the series. I was not the only consultant. The series consultant was Laura Silber, the Belgrade correspondent for the Financial Times, but the responsibility for the making of the programme lay with the series producer, Norma Percy, with the two programme producers and directors, Angus McQueen and Paul Mitchell. Although they would show -- they would have discussions with me and with others before making the programme and would show fine cuts of the programme to check certain things afterwards, the selection of material was theirs. It was their programme, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It was their programme. Thank you. Dr. Gow, I would like to take you then to another part, that is, scene 1 of the video tape we presented to the Registry. Actually, it is a copy but it is an easier way for us to handle. It is a copy of some remarks made by Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Kucan. It is scene No. 1 in our video tape. I would like you to look at it first, if I can have that on the screen, please? (The video clip was played) Dr. Gow, would you be able to reproduce the words of Mr. Milosevic in its original language? Perhaps I should give you a text in Serbo-Croatian of what is our understanding of what Mr. Milosevic says in the original language. Could you please, when this part is replayed, check whether this is correct, that you see whether these really are the words as used by Mr. Milosevic in this video tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will gladly do so. I can already tell you that they are not, but that is -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: This is just our transcript of what he said in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That, I think, should be marked and would be Defence 5, if you are going to offer it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we intend to do is to produce a few more things on this and either we use it as one exhibit or as three separate exhibits. It is the same to me. We have a practical problem. They have been stapled so they are one at this moment. Logically, I would say, it is one exhibit, but it will give first the Serbo-Croatian language. It then will give the text of the subtitles to check whether this is correct and then the third one I will ask a question of Dr. Gow, and I would say it is another text related to this part of the video film.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, might we be favoured with a copy if they are going to be introduced one after the other like this because we do not know what is coming up. If we could possibly see them, it would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not mind to separate them, your Honour. This would be then exhibit -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can separate it and call it Defence 5; if you want to, you could say Defence 5(A), then (B), (C).

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: 5(A) until (C) would be fine, as far as the Registry is concerned. (To the witness): So, Dr. Gow, I would like you to look at it again -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you still waiting for your copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, are you going to mark this as Defence 5(A)?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I will mark it as Defence 5(A).

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So, Dr. Gow, I would like you to view again the tape that has been, well, it is identical to what the Prosecution has shown us last week, and see whether the text we gave you is a correct version of what has already been said by Mr. Milosevic. Scene 1 again. Could we please see scene 1 again?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think they are trying to locate it now. (Scene 1 of the video was played)

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are these the wordings you understood to be spoken by Mr. Milosevic, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: They are? Then I would like you to look at another document, that would be Exhibit 5(B), which gives in writing the subtitles as they appear on the screen. Would you please, after having looked at the video, again tell us whether this is a correct -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 5(A) then is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can already tell you without looking at it that it is not, as I already indicated that I could, but I will look at it just to confirm. Without seeing the film again, this looks like the subtitles as I remember reading them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So you remember having seen these subtitles under the words of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case, and the subtitles are not a representation of the words which Milosevic is uttering at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So the subtitles are not really representing a fair translation of what Mr. Milosevic said, is that correct, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that that would be correct. They do not represent an exact translation of what he is saying. In the context of the interview with Milosevic, for the purposes of making the programme, he was asked at the time to give his version of the discussions with Kucan, President Kucan of Slovenia, the first scene against -- the two scenes were juxtaposed. The way this kind of programme is made is to interview all the parties at once and then to take one, and then another to tell the story through their own words. This is as far as I understand this method of journalism-come-documentary series making. The interview with Milosevic was asking him about the discussions with Kucan. It is clear that Milosevic, from the words which he actually says, is indicating the need to change the Yugoslav constitution. In the context of the interview, he is saying that he has no objection to Slovenes or, indeed, Croats becoming independent so long as -- I am paraphrasing a recollection -- all ethnic groups -- he uses "narod", but I think in this context it is fair to say, it would be correct to say, that he was making reference to ethnic groups -- are in the same position, that is, the need to change the constitution. The actual words that he utters, as on this frame, are something like, "Go on then, let us change the Yugoslav constitution so that we put all peoples in the same position, that we create a way to exercise the right to self-determination for all peoples on the same level". I am not sure if that is a perfect translation but, something like that. That is in the context of a further discussion, the questions around that, in which Milosevic is making clear that, according to the interpretation that he is giving, the significant problem for the SFRY was the effective power ---

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- because it was already concentrated in the republics, so in that case, in answer to your question ------

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if would you allow me ------

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Wait, wait. More than one person can speak at a time, but I think the court reporter can only take one down at a time. If you are objecting that the question (sic) is not responsive to your answer, then you make that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to object because the only question I put to Dr. Gow, whether this was a fair representation, a correct representation, of the subtitling in the video. What Dr. Gow does, as a matter of fact, is explaining why it is different. I was not that far yet. I only wanted to establish whether these were the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think he can answer your question and tell you "yes" or "no"; if he wants to explain his answer, I believe it is only fair to allow him to explain it. I suppose the problem is he is explaining it before he is answering it. Maybe you can say "yes" or "no", Dr. Gow, and then explain your answer. That might help because sometimes it is hard to find your answer among the words that you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you would allow me, I then want to present to Dr. Gow what is the correct translation, as far as we understand it, and perhaps then afterwards we come to questions on whether this is understandable, whether there were good reasons for it, or what might be the background of it. But I would first like to establish what has been said in Serbo-Croatian, how has it been subtitled and then what would be the correct translation of what has been said in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 5A is the subtitle in Serbo-Croatian and that has been admitted. Defence 5(B) will be admitted if no objection. Defence 5(B) then has been admitted and that is the translation of the subtitle that appeared in the video itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: 5(B) is the subtitles as shown in the video.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, as appeared, as shown in the video itself, fine. Dr. Gow has confirmed that the subtitle 5(B) is the subtitle that appeared in the video itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like present to him now 5(C) and ask Dr. Gow -- perhaps he should see the video again or just look at the Serbo-Croatian language that he agreed upon -- to see whether this would be a correct translation of the words that have been spoken in Serbo-Croatian by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might be permitted first to point out that my recollection of the previous -- my answer in response to the previous question was that I did clearly answer at the beginning, no, it was not fair and I gave the reason why it was not a fair representation to say that, and that was my understanding of the material that the people making the programme had and, therefore, that they were not necessarily unjustified in presenting it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is your explanation of why it was not the accurate translation. We understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, no, if I may ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the question was, was it a fair -- my recollection was that the question was, was it fair to say; and my answer was that it was not fair to say for the reasons that I gave. With regard to the translation with which I have just been provided -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you one moment. Is there an objection to what will be marked as Defence 5(C)?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 5(C) will be admitted. You may proceed, Dr. Gow, to refer to Defence 5(C).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The translation which I have been given is not substantially different from the translation which I think I offered from the Serbo-Croat text being given. The English is slightly -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there, in fact, a question regarding this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have questions on two. I am not interested to know all kinds of explanations, how television programmes are made, etc. I wanted to put two short questions to Dr. Gow and then, perhaps, a final third one.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you put the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. (To the witness): The first question is, Dr. Gow, is it correct to say that the subtitle translation speaks about republics where in the original language and in the final text the word "republics" is not used at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct and I believe I have already indicated that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is it also true, Dr. Gow, that in the subtitles the words "to succeed" are used where the literal translation speaks of "the right to self-determination"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My last question on this subject, your Honour, is have you not explained to us last week, Dr. Gow, that especially the subtleties in these contexts, republics, nations, peoples, self-determination, secession, these were vital importance for understanding the problem in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am no longer able to recall exactly what I said last week, but the meaning of anything that I was saying last week would be that it is very -- that it is of some importance to understand that in the final phases of the SFRY and the process of dissolution there were a number of arguments about these concepts and these terms, and that the facts of the matter were that the republics became independent on the basis of sovereignty and interpretations of the Yugoslav constitution on which all the parties, the Serbian leadership, the Slovenian leadership, all of them, agreed that the argument was on the same questions, the 1974 constitution, just that in some cases there were differing interpretations of the constitution and what their terms might mean, but that the use of those terms in some cases was ambiguous, in some cases elided two meanings. In those cases, the two meanings elided reflected (1) ethno-national interpretation, hence the use of the term "ethnic groups" in the subtitle here, I would believe, and with a second use which is "peoples" as it appears in international documentation. The facts of the matter are that on the basis of conventional, international practice, the republics became independent because conventionally the right to self-determination in the UN era at least has been practised with regard to peoples inhabiting territories rather than the ethno-national groups. So the facts of the matter were -- let me recapitulate to try to be clear -- there were arguments about the 1974 SFRY constitution and what the terms would mean. The SFRY dissolution occurred pursuant to those arguments which everybody agreed were about the same thing, just different interpretations of it. The international independence of those states was based, in part, on interpretations of the constitution, in part on the blending of aspects of public international law as understood by the European Community Arbitration Commission. I think the important fact of the matter is that the states became independent on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps a final question, your Honour: Dr. Gow, I would like only to pay attention to the linguistic aspects at this moment. Is it right that the subtitle gives a misrepresentation as far as especially these words "republics", "self-determination", "secessions" are concerned, the subtitling given misrepresentations of the precise words spoken by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The subtitling gives, the subtitling does not precisely reflect the words spoken either by Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Kucan but, nonetheless, reflects the character of the discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to take Dr. Gow, I would like to take you now, to the last part of our video presented to the Registry and that is No. 2, scene No. 2. (Scene No. 2 of the video was played) (To the witness): Dr. Gow, could you please tell us whether this is the context in which those parts we discussed earlier are put in this film? The part about Seselj we discussed I think it was Thursday; you have commented on some of these statements of Mr. Seselj. We have then shown to you. Are these the accompanying parts of that film "The Death of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, if I have understood your question, then when I was giving evidence there were some extracts of Borisav Seselj making comments, some of those extracts are part of the extended sequence that you have just shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the context in which these fragments are presented in the original film "The Death of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clearly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you please identify a few persons for us I heard the name of Mr. Reihl-Kir; is it true that he was the Chief of police in eastern Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Dr. Gow, who is Mr. Glavas, whether his position is correctly given in this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall what his position was given as being in the video. My recollection is that he had the position of being leader of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Community, Hrvatska Demokratska Zajednica, the party of president Franjo Tudjman in Osijek in eastern Slovenia, and he was also, I think, a Deputy Commander of the local either police, special forces, or Territorial Defence. I do not recall precisely any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, Mr. Susak, could you tell us who he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gojko Susak is presently Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, Mr. Boljkovac, who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of which we are speaking, he was, I think, the Interior Minister for the Republic of Croatia. I am not sure what his position is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Does this clip, Dr. Gow, not clearly indicate that the Croatian government had no intention whatsoever to prevent clashes to occur trying to get rid of someone who tried to prevent them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think it does that. I think the fact that Boljkovac is testifying here would suggest that it was not a matter for the Croatian government. On the other hand, the role identified for Susak and the role identified for Glavas would indicate that elements within the HDZ certainly would have had that perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So there were members of government that had no intention whatsoever to prevent these clashes to occur; you are making a distinction between the whole government and members -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the government and between members of the government party. Mr. Glavas was not a member of the government but he was a member of the HDZ, which was the party of -- the majority party which was forming the government at the time and the party of the President, Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Susak was close to Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Susak was reported as being very close to Mr. Tudjman and continues to be reported to be close, perhaps even closer, to Mr. Tudjman. Mr. Susak -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: He is presented as one of the persons responsible for not preventing these clashes to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would go beyond that and say that he is presented, not only as a person who was not preventing the clashes, but a person who, as I understand the presentation, was involved in firing rocket grenades at Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you answered already my next question which was that does it not also indicate that the Croatian government, while at least Mr. Susak was close to Mr. Tudjman, violently provoked the Serbs by attacking them with rockets, Serbs that at that time were trying to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not entirely clear again that that is exactly what it is showing. It was a very complex situation. The incident in which Mr. Susak is reported, almost shown, to have participated in firing rocket grenades at Borovo Selo, was already in response to actions taken by Serbs in the area erecting barricades. That was part of a very complex situation which had been taking place on the territories of the Republic of Croatia from the summer of 1990 onwards. I believe in testimony and certainly in my writings, I have indicated that in part, those actions taken by the Serbs in those parts of Croatia were in response to government restructuring of the Interior Ministry, for example, closing down the police station in Knin, effectively removing local Serbs from being in charge of the police force, taking it to another location -- in the case of Knin I think it is Benkovac, but I do not remember precisely any more. There were a series of concerns. In response to those concerns, the Serbs in a number of areas began to erect barricades and to create what were, effectively, no-go areas. In the whole of this period, the Croatian Interior Ministry at the time of the Borovo Selo incident, my recollection is it was suggested that there had been 180 armed violent incidents on the territory of Republic of Croatia in the preceding six or nine months -- I forget the exact time frame. The situation in Croatia at the time was very complex, as I say. There were small groups from both ethnic Serbian and ethnic Croatian backgrounds who, I believe, were driving around in certain areas who were harassing houses of those on the other side at night. I cannot say that I have evidence, but my suspicion is that political authorities and official bodies on both the Serbian and Croatian side were, to some extent, indulgent of this. People like Reihl-Kir were doing their best to try to mediate the situation and to mitigate these developments. In that situation, what is clear is that although there were incidents of these kinds, they were on a scale perhaps with incidents in Northern Ireland in my own country, and the reason for an escalation from a situation in which there was low level, local violence of the kind experienced in Northern Ireland to a situation in which barricades were being erected in which large elements of armed force were beginning to be arranged either with local Serbs or with assistance of the JNA in Croatia and later in Bosnia -- I am sorry, it is another of my long sentences; I have forgotten where I began. If I may try to break it down, the situation in Northern Ireland maybe a parallel to the level of violence which was in Croatia at the time we are talking about; small groups intimidating members of opposing communities. Some people, such as Reihl-Kir, was seeking to calm that situation down. Quite clearly, there was a degree of support or indulgence from the authorities on both sides. It is my suspicion, I cannot say that I have specific evidence for it, but if we take the clips from Death of Yugoslavia for evidence, we see both evidence that Seselj with support from the Serbian Interior Ministry and the support of Susak in this area indicates elements of those in official positions supporting this. The difference between that level of violence and the escalation to one in which you have largely armed populations, the use of the JNA to assist the Serbs in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the beginnings of a project which is, effectively, to expand the political territory dominated and controlled by the Republic of Serbia, in effect, is the difference made by the presence of the JNA constituting an armed force which would lead from low level violence of the kind in Northern Ireland to major armed hostilities which constitute a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, as a matter of fact, to make myself clear to you, the questions I am putting to you at this moment deal with the way the material has been presented by the Prosecution. I am not asking you to go in any detail on whatever may be said on what happened in that territory at that time. I am concentrating on the material that has been presented in examination-in-chief, and that is what my questions are, perhaps for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, I thought you asked me about the involvement of Susak and Glavas. I am sorry if I have misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will explain to you then that some parts of a video have been shown to us indicating what Mr. Seselj did with his paramilitary groups in Croatia. What I am trying to do at this moment is to put us in the context as it has been presented in the film. That also is my next question, Dr. Gow: Does this video clip in this context not indicate that the reasons, and I remind you that Seselj said that the people in Borovo Selo turned to Belgrade for prosecution, so that the reasons given in this programme for calling Seselj to Borovo Selo were left out in those portions of this programme that has been presented before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are asking me -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can interrupt? Do you really need to get that from the witness? That is a submission you will make and it seems to me pretty obvious that you are correct, but need you really go into cross-examination on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my problem is that what seems obvious to quite many people now and then, does not always seem to be obvious for the witness. That is the reason why I am putting this question, because if it is obvious for you, then perhaps I will leave this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps I should only speak for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It was obvious to me because I asked, I think, the witness a question that was directly related to this. That had to do with the foundation for his testimony Friday, or I guess it was Thursday, that Serbia was supporting paramilitary activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I had asked him was it not true that all the video we had seen really related to the conflict between Serbia and Croatia. Then I believe after recess the Prosecution played a portion at the end of either part 3 or part 4 of their Exhibit 30 or 31 where there was a single mention of, the Prosecution said, Bosnia, and the witness said that that related to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and when Seselj said that, he said he had checked to verify what he was talking about and he was really talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina. He never told us who he checked with, and I do not know whether he spoke with Mr. Seselj or somewhere else, but he did come back and say that he had checked it. But you are right, everything else related to Croatia and Serbia. I am sorry, I am making it longer -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But if it relates to Borovo Selo, first of all, it is Croatia. My major aim at this moment is to make clear that whatever Mr. Seselj did and is said to have done in this screen that there might be reasons for doing so without being shown on this clip.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, but ..... MR. ORIE (To the witness): Dr. Gow, do you think that this information, reasons, why people called him to Borovo Selo is important for a fair evaluation of the pictures you have given your testimony on last Thursday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I think it is ------

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you think that the information is important for a fair evaluation of those pictures shown to us, Mr. Seselj telling what he did, he has now given the reasons why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I did not ask whether it was necessary; I asked whether it was important for a fair evaluation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure -- I am not sure that it is important for a fair evaluation of the information as was originally presented. I would say two things about that: The first was that it was a decision that myself and the Office of the Prosecutor not to show extended extracts in which commentary appeared; only to show the words of the protagonists themselves. The second is that in that context the words of the protagonist, Vojislav Seselj, were being used to indicate the links of his paramilitary group with official Serbian organs. In that context, I think that is what it did and it is not important to a fair interpretation of that piece of information. When I was asked about it by Judge McDonald in questioning, I indicated, first of all, not that I had gone away and checked, but that Seselj himself said there were Bosnian Serbs there, and so forth; "We were there". The most important groups were the Serbian Interior Ministry forces, and what I said later after the recess was that I had checked and that he was making reference to the town of Zvornik in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which I believe you would see if you were to run the whole of that tape. In saying that, the point was to demonstrate the link between Seselj and Serbian official bodies. I think it did that, and it is not important to understand the context. When Judge McDonald did ask me, I explained that it was referring to an incident at Borovo Selo and I described something of that incident. Had I been asked to do so, I would have been perfectly happy to go on for a lot longer to explain the full context as presented in the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you have just told us that the Prosecution would rather not show parts of the film giving comments. Are you aware of any comments taken out in the parts that have been shown last week to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that commentary -- and I make a distinction between commentary and comments -- was taken out specifically so that only the words of the protagonists themselves would appear. Occasionally, you will have noticed that the end of the commentary appears and is cut off. That is in the nature of producing these things. I am not aware of the specific portions of commentary which are missing. In many cases, those portions of commentary would have assisted me in giving evidence, for example, on the case of Seselj making reference to Zvornik, because the commentary makes it clear that he is talking about Zvornik. I am not an expert in the practice of either criminal Tribunals or international criminal Tribunals, and in seeking to use evidence I was taking the advice of the Office of the Prosecutor in what would be an appropriate manner in which to behave -- not that I wish to -- I am just trying to make this clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, so it was not difficult to take out comments, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that that is what I am saying and I am not sure in what sense you use the word "difficult".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is it possible to take out comments if you want to take them out in order to give a fair picture of what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in the video suite preparing the tape and doing the editing. I would guess that it is not very easy to do all that editing to try to get extracts which are only people speaking which do not have the commentary on them; it would be far easier to let the commentary run, but I think, my understanding of the advice I was getting from the Office of the Prosecutor was that it would be philosophically unsound to allow the commentary to run in a way which would then, perhaps, pre-empt or prejudice what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But they finally succeeded in taking out those comments they did not want to be in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there ------

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the question. It is quite clear the witness is indicating that on our advice there were segments taken out which were overvoice or commentary. The witness has said this numerous times. Now it has been put to him, suggested, that we are taking out those parts which we did not want. The witness is clearly indicating that all of the parts which related to overvoice, as it is often referred to, were taken out where it was possible to do so. I object to any question which suggests that it was selectively done, that overvoice was selectively done for some sort of prejudicial reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I listened carefully to what the witness told me. Part of his answer was that he was not very clear on that, that perhaps part of the sequence we showed you today has been taken out because they wanted to avoid any commentary in there. So what I was trying to demonstrate, and that was the reason for my questions, is to establish on whether you want to show them something without the commentary, whether you are able to do so and especially whether the Prosecution is able to take out the commentary. We have seen at the end of last week that they successfully achieved that. That is what I want to establish, because the witness suggested, at least, that this part might not have been shown because of the commentary in it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Your question is -- it is time for lunch, it is 10 minutes past actually -- what in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My question, since he gave this as a possible reason for not including this part in the video clip that has been presented by the Prosecutor, since he suggested there might have been the reason not to show us part with commentary in it, I wanted to establish whether you can take it out and whether actually the Prosecution has taken out, where necessary, those comments from the video tape.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Whether the Prosecution in the clips they showed us included any commentary?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Or whether this has been taken out, and that is my suggestion, where they wanted to avoid the commentary in the video clip.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will ask one more question, then we really must recess for lunch. I think you have made your point though. One more on this point and then we will recess for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think I have four or five or six more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not want to make you selectively select your questions, so we will stand in recess until 2.30 for lunch. (1.15 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.30 p.m.) PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Orie, you are standing because you were going to continue with the witness, but I see Mr. Niemann is standing too, so he must want to say something about your intentions. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We wish to raise an objection to any line of questioning which, in our submission, amounts to nothing more than an objection to the admissibility or otherwise of the Prosecution exhibit taken at this late stage. In our submission, the line of questioning directed towards the witness prior to the luncheon adjournment was really a comment upon either the lack of completeness or, alternatively, that somehow or other we have unfairly manipulated the presentation of this evidence. If it is either of those grounds, then, your Honours, this is not a matter that should fairly be laid at the feet of the witness. If the Defence wish to object to the exhibit on either of those grounds, then let them raise the objection and we will deal with that. In our submission, your Honour, what we were trying to in the way we presented the evidence was to remove comments by the BBC commentators so that your Honours would be presented with only the words of the particular speaker rather than present what the BBC commentators' views were. If the Defence feels that they should be included, then by all means let them include them, but it is, in our submission, inappropriate and unfair to ask the witness to deal with and contend with matters which really amount to nothing more than prosecutorial decisions. Finally, your Honours, in our submission, the whole basis upon which the Prosecution Exhibit 31 part 2 was tendered seems to have been lost in all this. We tendered the exhibit for the purposes of showing the participation of Serb paramilitary not as an effort to demonstrate that either Serbia or Croatia were responsible for commencement of the war. So we object to it on that ground too, that, in our submission, it seems to be being misrepresented. So, your Honour, that is the basis of my objection to that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I have to emphasise that the Defence was not aware of taking out some comments of this programme. We have seen the whole five hours of tapes, of course, but we were not aware when we did not object against the admissibility of this tape that it was not exactly what we had before. Apart from that, I hope you will understand that it is a bit difficult if it is just roughly indicated on what part it is, that before having seen it as a whole, it is difficult for us to say, well, it is incomplete or not; perhaps we should do so, but then we should play the whole part of this video before we can express ourselves on whether we think this is a admissible evidence or not because it might be distorted, taken out of its context, et cetera whatever. These are my two main, general observations to that issue. Of course, we were in a rather specific position during the last few days because, on the one hand, of course, I do agree that it is the selection of the Prosecutor's team what to present and what not to present, on the other hand, the witness has indicated that he was a consultant when producing this programme. So it is perhaps a very specific situation that might not be there any more in the coming days and the coming months perhaps. That caused us some problems in what questions could still be put to the witness or not, because he is not responsible for the selection, I do agree with that, but he had some involvement in the producing of the programme and, to that extent, questions about the framework, the context in which certain parts shown to us have to be put, we thought could be validly put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know that he was not involved in the selections of the portions to play. I do not know. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, were you at all involved with the Prosecutor in making a decision as to certain portions of the video to play?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, your Honour. I identified areas in which matters of relevance were being expressed by the individuals in question. It was -- again I am not sure if it is, I will do so because your Honour asks, but I am still not sure that it is appropriate for me to be answering the question beyond that, but it was the decision of the Office of the Prosecutor to exclude the portions on which commentary appeared, and to restrict the extracts shown to those in which the protagonists themselves were uttering words.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I certainly would not ask you to reveal ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was involved in discussions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- the content of those discussions or anything that the Prosecutor may have told you or what you told the Prosecutor in terms of preparation because I think that would be inappropriate. I was asking you only whether you were involved in the discussions because it seems to me that the question goes to the selection and whether there was some bias in the selection. It seems to me that seemed to be the suggestion of the Defence. If you were involved in the selection, then, of course, it may go to whether or not you potentially may have some bias or why did you make this particular selection? Why did you omit this segment and why did you omit another segment? It seems to me that might be relevant. This is an exhibit, this is a film, a five part film. It seems to me when you offer a portion of it, the other portion or, at least, other portions of it may be offered by the opposing side for completeness purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So he, of course, is free to do that. Just like any document, if you offer one page, he can then offer the other pages. That is fair game. The question is whether or not he may question this witness about why something was omitted, I gather; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It seems to me that if that witness participated in that decision, then it may be fair game.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, but, your Honour, I make it very clear it was my decision to take out the overvoice. I said to the witness at the time the overvoice must be taken out because we only want to present that part of the evidence which relates to the person speaking. It was my decision. Therefore, I submit, your Honour, it was unfair that the witness should be asked to justify that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is really a question as to whose credit this cross-examination goes and it may goes to yours rather than the witness; that is what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Exactly, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. As to this question, it appears that we now know that the Prosecutor solely made the decision in question that you are now questioning this witness about. So it is inappropriate, but we did learn that Dr. Gow did make some decisions with respect to which segments to include or portions to include or exclude. So it seems to me if you ask him first and he has participated in the decision, then this line of questioning is appropriate; if he has not participated in the decision, then it is inappropriate. You, of course, are totally free to add any portion of the five part series that you consider is appropriate for completeness sake. But just do not question this witness and do not put it to this witness as to why this decision was made if he did not make the decision. The Prosecutor said that the decision now that is being discussed was not made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not aware -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you want to ask the witness, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have no rememberance of specifically asking the "why" question, but the issue has been clarified and the Defence has considered its position during the lunch break. Since we have no further questions for Dr. Gow, it is not a problem for us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, thank you, Mr. Orie. Mr. Niemann, do you have additional questions on redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, your Honour. Redirect by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, during the course of cross-examination your attention was drawn to a particular article that you had written entitled "The Hissing Snake". I think the full title was "Serbian Nationalism and the Hissssing Ssssnake in the International Order: Whose sovereignty? Which nation?" Mr. Orie then took you to several parts of the article, some of which have been marked but, in particular, he took you to a paragraph which starts on page 457, the final paragraph: "The hissing snake peculiar to the Yugoslav context, the inspirational serpent, is that of Serbian nationalism", and so forth and goes on. What, Dr. Gow, is the intent and purpose of your article to focus on the issue and question of nationalism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intent of the article is to examine the questions posed for international order of situations in which there are violent manifestations of nationalism following the collapse of the communist order in central and Eastern Europe in particular, although not exclusively. Often in the course of my testimony so far, discussion has been made of various concepts, the four Ss, to which the "hissssing ssssnake" refers; sovereignty, self-determination, statehood and security. I think you will -- I would have thought, as far as I am able to judge what I wrote myself, that the intent, and I would like to think achievement, of the writing is a discussion of those concepts as issues of international order, and the springboard for that discussion was the Yugoslav context, but the weight of the article was not so much to the Yugoslav context but to the understanding of those issues which has emerged from the dissolution of Yugoslavia and, in particular, with regard to possible interpretations of the position of sovereignty and self-determination, but beyond that the need for security. I hope that is an adequate answer. It was, essentially, a discussion of international order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was it in any way an expression of your feelings of your likes or dislikes of the Serbian people or their nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have thought that it was quite clearly not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In part because there is no real discussion that I would characterise as being of that nature. The early parts of the article which indicate the original idea for using the metaphor the four Ss -- the sibilant Ss of my playful "hissing snake" -- was the position of the Serbs in Yugoslavia, that Yugoslavia had been a state in which they would all have the opportunity of ruling together, and dissolution of Yugoslavia provided a situation in which if with the independence of the states as by the time I was writing had long been established -- if the independence of the states was established, and that had long been the case by the time I was writing, then this would mean that the Serbs who had seen the formation of the Federation as a framework for all living in one overall community no longer would be in that situation. As far as I recall, and I did have a chance to glance over it while I was looking at it on the table here the other day, I do express the view of the genuine fears, that there were genuine fears, of Serbs in this situation, but this does not mitigate the decisions of those responsible in the Serbian leadership for the things that happened afterwards or in the course of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Also in cross-examination, Dr. Gow, you were asked by Mr. Orie about a military unit known as the "Green Berets". Do you recall being questioned on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: And where, in fact, they were located throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina during the period 1992 and onwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware, Dr. Gow, whether or not they were trained, armed and equipped in an equivalent way or otherwise to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am certainly aware that they were not equipped or armed in an equivalent way to the JNA or to its putative successor in the VRS. On the question of training, as some of them had no doubt been in the JNA at some stage, it would not be correct entirely to say that they did not have the same training, that they were not the same kind of organisation. Equally, I would point out that in the spring of 1992 my recollection is that these organisations, relatively small, were present in a number of locations as I indicated, were not necessarily significantly armed and that, as far as the JNA was concerned, another organisation which I do not think either myself or Mr. Orie mentioned, the Patriot League (which was again, I think primarily Muslim but also had Serbs and Croats in it) was seen as far more of a concern to the JNA. I recall some time in the early part of 1992, The Army Weekly, Narodna Armija, expressing some concern about the formation of the Patriotic League. I cannot say that it did not express any concern about Green Berets, but I do not remember reading about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Also in cross-examination you were shown a number of Defence exhibits, namely, 5(A), 5(B) and 5(C), which related to a speech, or part of a speech, by Slobodan Milosevic; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure to what you refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You were taken to the commentary or I should say the subtitling that appeared on that speech by Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to the extract that was played in which Presidents Kucan and Milosevic were juxtaposed, then, yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, with your experience in dealing with translations and interpretations, particularly in your case from the Serbo-Croatian language to the English language, do you understand the difference between interpretation and translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand there to be a difference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what your understanding of the difference is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I find it difficult but, if you wish, I can try. "Translation" would be to give an accurate, as far as possible accurate, and verbatim record of the words uttered. "Interpretation" would be both to use words in the translation which would accurately reflect the nature of the material being discussed, what the person being translated was saying, rather than necessarily the words themselves which are being used. It is a very difficult problem for a translator. I live with a translator. I know it is a problem that is faced all the time; how you deal with these kinds of problems. "Interpretation", therefore, could either on one level be the interpretation of the intent of the speaker and, therefore, the choice of particular words for a particular translation. For example, when we looked at that particular extract, the exhibit you talked about, when I read the original Serbo-Croat, I think I used the word -- did I use the word "implement", I am not sure, or may be "execute" with regard to the right to self-determination, and I think the translation offered said "utilizing". Again, it is a question of the choice of a particular word which in this case, I think, made no substantive difference to the sense; in some cases a substantive difference might arise from the particular choice of words. Therefore, it is important for the translator to interpret the sense which is intended to be conveyed by the speaker. The final level of interpretation -- that was one level -- the other level of interpretation, of course, is simply to take what is said and to give it interpretation rather than interpret within the translation being made. But I am not a translator myself, so excuse me if I do not understand the practice correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We have no further questions of Dr. Gow, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to Dr. Gow being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. You are excused. Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I call Dragan Lukac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, while we are waiting for Mr. Lukac to come in, I reviewed your witness list, your proposed witness list, of "will call" and "may call" and tried to add up the time. The time comes to a potential of four months to six months, assuming five hour days, four days a week; six months if it is a maximum, four months if it is a minimum. I would like you to take a check on those figures for me and we will talk about it before we adjourn tonight. The witness DRAGAN LUKAC was called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, there should be in front of you an oath which I would like you to take.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I ask Miss Sutherland to close down the machine because my view of the witness is obstructed?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukac, would you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Lukac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 16th October 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born at Bosanski Samac in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you study philosophy and sociology in Sarajevo from 1975 to 1979?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Upon graduation did you go back to Bosanski Samac to work where you continued to work up until the commencement of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For a period of time did you work as a political consultant where you counselled various socio-political organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you also in the military, Mr. Lukac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For what period of time were you in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the military from 1982 till 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attend the reserve officers school in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you acquire the rank of reserve Lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reserve 2nd Lieutenant which is the lowest officer grade -- rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the way that the Yugoslav military forces were structured during that period of time, and I am speaking during the 1980s up to 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the whole organisational structure of the JNA or in a particular area?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am just asking you very generally what was the way it was structured? There was the JNA and was there any other form of defence system operational in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You probably mean of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at that time which had two parts, the JNA and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the different roles that were played by either arm of the military forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA was the active military, active army, mostly professional, and the Territorial Defence represented a second aspect of the armed forces, the reserve forces of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, which was preparing for the defence of the country in case of an outside aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from your involvement in the military, were you also involved in the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, since 16th February 1982, that was the date when I started to work for the Secretariat of the Internal Affairs in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is the Secretariat of Internal Affairs commonly referred to as the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you an inspector in the criminal investigation in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was an inspector in the criminal police of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then did you rise to the position of Acting Chief of police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1st January 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then subsequently proposed for the position of Chief of police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, that is on 17th December 1986, the previous secretary of the SUP of Bosnia, of Bosanski Samac, was dismissed. He was the Secretary of the League of the Communists of Bosanski Samac. He was a Croat and so somebody else had to be on this post. I was a candidate because a Croat was needed, but certain forces were against and prevented me to becoming the head of the SUP. Instead of me on 1st July 1987, a Serb, Radovan Antic, was chosen to be at that particular post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think from what you said your nationality is Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Instead of being appointed to the position of chief of police, were you subsequently appointed to the position of Chief of the Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the Head of the Public Security which is the second commanding post in the police structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you maintain that position then, there and after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remained in that position up until 1989 or 1990 when the restructuring of the police in Bosnia-Herzegovina occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then there was restructuring. The Republic Secretariat for Internal Affairs was changed into the Ministries of the Internal Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and up until then the Municipal police was under the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then when this change took place, this restructuring took place, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was then appointed the Chief of the Criminal Division in the police station of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I want to turn now, if I may, to the events of 1992 and beyond, but leading up to the commencement of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were you still working at the police station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in a position, being a member of the community, to observe what was happening in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in a position because I was following the media on both sides, and you have to know that Bosanksi Samac is at the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. That was why I had some information concerning the events on the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what the position was with respect to the position with the JNA and its leadership in relation to the Croatian and Serbian conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1991 the JNA committed aggression on to the Republic of Croatia with the aim to realise the plan of creating a greater Serbia on the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this have any impact upon the area where you were located in northern Bosnia, in the Bosanski Samac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the consequence of this was that the JNA acted on the territory of Bosnian Posavina, which is a territory in the north east of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in the latter half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what their involvement was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As it is known, the attack by the JNA on to the Republic of Croatia came from various directions. The basic aim was to cut the territory of the Republic of Croatia because of its shape in several parts, and in that way it would have been easier to occupy particular areas. This attack was especially intense in the eastern part of the Republic of Croatia. So there was the front line going from the towns of Zupanja, Vinkovci, in Vukovar and in Osijek. Taking into account that the JNA was not able to clench the defence and the resistance of the Croatian defenders and in that area from Bosnia and Herzegovina tried to create a way to enter the Republic of Croatia and to cut off certain parts of these areas. So, some pockets were created, as it is known in military terminology, and so these pockets were created to quench the resistance by the Croats. One of those pockets was envisaged by the JNA in the area where I lived, that was in the area of Bosanksi Samac. What is important is that that particular area was chosen because at that time on the River Sava which divides, which represents the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were only two bridges left on which the equipment, military equipment, and weaponry could have been transferred. One of those bridges was at Bosanski Samac. The JNA concentrated certain forces at the end of July and early August 1991 in Bosanski Posavina. That came from the Tuzla corps, the headquarters of which was in Tuzla, and the commander of the Tuzla corps was Sava Jankovic, a General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tuzla is in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The bridge at Bosanski Samac bridges the Sava River from Bosnia-and Herzegovina into Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is also a bridge which carries road communications, that is, vehicles and railways, a railway bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to the headquarters in Posavina, was there also a garrison in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that larger area where we were, the only barracks, that is, a garrison, the only barracks, was in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Brcko is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is also on the border with the Republic of Croatia below the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the name of the JNA's group that was located in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Tuzla corps deployed the commanding structure in our area in the village of Pelagicevo in the Gradacac municipality. The, name, the working name, that was given to this commanding place was the 17th Operational Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What municipalities, if you can recall, were the 17th Operational Tactical Group responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 17th Operational Tactical Group of the JNA from the Tuzla corps had the responsibility for the zone of six municipalities in our areas, that is, the municipalities of Brcko, Orasje, Bosanski Samac, Modrica, Gradacac and Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the Commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commanding structure was in the village of Pelagicevo which belonged to the municipality of Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where he was born or where he came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander of the 17th Operational Tactical Group was the Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, Lieutenant Colonel of the JNA, and he was located in the village of Pelagicevo. He was born in Sombor and lived in, was resident of the town of Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where are those two towns, Sombor and Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sombor and Kragujevac are towns in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why was the town of Pelagicevo chosen for the headquarters of 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have got an opinion about why Pelagicevo was chosen. I think it was for three reasons. First of all, the village itself is located in the centre of the area of responsibility of the six municipalities covered by the 17th Tactical Operational Group; the second reason being that some 20 kilometres from this village was the barracks belonging to the Brcko garrison, and at the same time this village is located nearby the main road, Orasje Tuzla, because of the rapidity of the logistic support coming that had to be ensured from the Tuzla corps. There might have been another reason, that is, while during the Second World War in this particular village the Chetnik headquarters were located, and I think that from morale reasons of the members -- it was chosen because of the morale reasons of the members of this particular group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any military establishment in Bosanski Samac itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander of the 17th Operational Tactical group created a military structure on the territory of all these six municipalities. So, on the territory of the municipality of Bosanksi Samac, there were units created at the level of the brigade in three Serbian villages. In the first phase there were the commanding structures of battalions. They used to be called the 1st, the 2nd and the 3rd Company. At the end of January 1992 and beginning of February 1992, a fourth company was created in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1991 was there a change by the headquarters of the JNA in the structure of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May 1991, the General of the JNA, the General of the JNA in Belgrade, took a decision concerning not taking -- exclusion of all the Registry evidence concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina, concerning all the conscripts in a particular municipality. Such a decision taken by the general headquarters of the JNA was against the constitution because, according to the constitution, these administrations were in the responsibility of a particular republic. In July 1991, JNA had implemented this decision by the general headquarters of the JNA, and they did so by taking by force from the Secretariat of the Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina and for various municipalities it took all the documentation, including Bosanksi Samac as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just tell me where was the headquarters of the JNA that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say the decision taken, are you referring to the fact that the recruitment or conscription of people for the JNA was from that time on to be handled directly by the JNA itself rather than through the Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that prior to that time, I take it then, that whenever conscripts for the JNA were required, this was a matter that was organised through the Republic's government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was done through the Secretariat for Defence, that is, the Ministry for Defence. That was an integral part of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have touched on just a moment ago the two tiers of the military forces, the JNA and the TO. Are you aware from your experience in the military of Yugoslavia what the intended purpose of the TO was to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Practically, by taking the register, the register of the JNA in the way that I have just described, the Territorial Defence structure was abolished in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That means that the JNA had all the register of all the conscripts, and so they could create a structure of the army on the territory of every municipality and that is what they did precisely in the area of Bosanski Samac. The units that were formed exclusively contained the members of the Serbian people, and the structure that resulted from it, the military structure, was drawn from the people, from the people from the villages with Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have answered the question I was going to ask you. I would like to go back, if I may, to the original purpose, as you understood it, for the Territorial Defence in terms of what the military strategy of this organisation was to be in the defence of Yugoslavia. Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the Territorial Defence before all these changes and decisions taken by the general headquarters of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. If you could answer that question in relation to prior to the events of the JNA taking the process of conscription into its own hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose for the existence of the Territorial Defence that existed in the previous period as a part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia was the use of these forces in the case of an external aggression on Yugoslavia, which would have meant that, together with the JNA, the Territorial Defence had to defend the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the TO subordinate to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in the previous period was organised on a Republican basis. In the commanding post, it had the Republican level, a regional level and a municipality level. On a Republic and a regional level, there was always an active officer from the JNA who was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
