utterances.text: Do you say that it is through the infusion of this position of the JNA officer at this level that meant that ultimately the TO was commanded by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was practically under the command of the organs of the Republic, that is, the government and the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in state of war it would have been under some subordinate command to the JNA, especially if the JNA would have been on the same territory as the Territorial Defence and they would act together, then the JNA would have a higher commanding level than the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was the Territorial Defence financed, or perhaps I should say -- yes, who financed the Territorial Defence, might be a better question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was solely financed from the budgets of the municipalities, that is, first of all, from the tax that is paid by the people who lived in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sort of weaponry was the Territorial Defence equipped with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence at the level of municipality in our area had infantry weapons and lighter artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you just assist us for those of us who do not know these terms too well what this consists of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was semi-automatic and automatic infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was this weaponry of the Territorial Defence stored?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This weaponry up until 1990 was in the storage houses of the Territorial Defence in every municipality, and in 1992 it was, that was organised by the JNA and all the weaponry was taken out from the storage houses and taken to an unknown location without any consultation with the authorities of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you say that this happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was done in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this seen by you and others in the local areas as an unusual step to be taken by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not only an unusual step, it was also against the law. Such a decision could have been taken only by the municipality organisation for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What effect did taking these weapons from the TO have on the local community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the peoples who lived in that territory, on the territory of our municipality, interpreted precisely in the following way this decision that it was not legal and the weapons belonged to the people which was illegally taken from the people who lived in that area, and that was done without any decision of the legitimate representative of those peoples at the level of municipality and, in any case, it introduced a level of uncertainty in the area of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately what the population of Bosanski Samac was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, according to the last census from 1991, there were some 34,000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just very approximately, are you able to tell us what the ethnic breakdown of the population was of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to that census, there were 45 per cent Croats, 41 per cent Serbs and 6.8 Muslims and the rest belonged to other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall when the first democratic elections were held in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first democratic elections were done, multi-party elections, were done at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you aware of the names of the political parties or the major political parties that participated in this election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina participated a large number of political parties that had been created. I think that it is important to speak about six political parties that after the elections had received more votes. First of all, the Croatian Democratic Union, then the party of Democratic Action, the Serbian Democratic Party, the Social Democratic Party, the Liberal Party and the party of Reform. In the municipality of Bosanski Samac the six parties were represented in the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And by "municipal government" what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not the town but it was the municipality government. They had a municipality government and a municipality parliament. One should say that the municipality of Bosanski Samac was made out of the town of Bosanski Samac plus the 26 villages that belonged to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The political parties that you just mentioned a moment ago in your evidence, were those political parties also represented on a Republic-wide level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were represented also in Republican level; they might not have been in the same proportion at the level of the national parliament, but as it was the case in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the party to receive most of the votes in the 1990 election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the election results in the territory of Bosanki Samac Municipality, members of the Croatian Democratic Union took up most of the seats in the municipal assembly. Out of 50 members of our municipal assembly, the Croatian Democratic Union had 21 representatives; the second best represented party was the Serbian Democratic Party which had 17 representatives; the third party was the Social Democratic Party with six representatives; the fourth one was the Reform Party with three representatives; the fifth was the Party of Democratic Action with two representatives;,and then the Liberal Party with one representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were these people then represented in the municipal government in terms of representatives from each of the political parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ratio of seats distributed in Parliament I have just mentioned, and at the municipal level the party, that is, at the local level, the parties agreed how to distribute individual posts among them in the territory of the municipality so that the President of the municipality became Marto Nujic representing the Croatia Democratic Union, Dr. Blagoje Simic of the Serb Democratic Party became his deputy, Mirko Jovanovic, representative of the Serb Democratic Party, became the head of the local government, and then his deputy became Mr. Itzebegovic representing the Party for Democratic Action, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The last gentleman you referred to, Itzebegovic, was he in any way related to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are relations, rather, their fathers are brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that fathers and brothers or father and son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are sons of two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the political structure there, apart from the representatives of the political parties, were there any other representatives that were involved in the local municipal administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not quite understand your question. Will you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the police in any way represented in the local administration of affairs in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the territory of Bosanski Samac municipality, as I have said, as of 1989, there was a police Station as a part, as a unit, of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. During the multi-party elections, the parties, the multi-political parties, agreed to designate a representative of the Croat Democratic union as the head of the police, and the security, I mean the uniformed branch, its head was designated by the Serb Democratic Party. That was in agreement with the orders of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the understanding of the political parties at republican level, which was that on the basis of the results of elections at the republican level and on the basis of the local agreement at the local level should appoint only two head officers in the local police. The Commander of the police Station became Vinko Dragicevic. He was appointed by the Croat Democratic Union and Milan Jekic became the head of the local uniformed branch of the police on behalf of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did these two gentlemen continue to retain office? For how long did these two gentlemen continue to retain office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They remained both in the office until 30th March 1992. Then they submitted their resignations to these officers and that was when the term of office ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to this, in December 1991, was action taken by the Serbian representatives in the Opstina of Bosanski Samac with respect to the Opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, and it relates to the establishment of the Serb Opstina of Samac in the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality, I believe it needs to be pointed out that a Serb parliament was set up in the territory of the so-called Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina established at the time, and in conformity with the decisions of the so-called Serb parliament in Serb Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serb Opstina Bosanksi Samac was founded in the municipality of Bosanski Samac in December 1991. The Serb parliament, the Serb government, and some departments were established which the municipality needed which meant, to all intents and purposes, the establishment of parallel authority in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "parallel", are you referring to the fact that the municipal government established as a consequence of the election as opposed to a special Serb municipal government side by side with that which took place in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the results of the elections, all the official bodies were set up in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, so that parliament, the government, and they were, and all the political parties, rather, all the three peoples living in the territory were represented there; so that the establishment of the Serb parliament and government in Bosanski Samac Opstina meant setting up a parallel system of authority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this act and other matters create tension between the ethnic community in Bosanksi Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did create a certain atmosphere by which showed mistrust, mutual mistrust, because the other two peoples living in the area, the Muslim and the Croat peoples, were caught unawares by this move of the representatives of the Serb people, and such a move or other disestablishment of such parallel authority, it was thought could serve no purpose. That is what was thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a consequence of this tension, was the police Force of which you were a member given any special orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, no, no special orders were received. They were not ordered to take any special, any specific measures, but as the tension grew in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, late 1991, all of the police Force was mobilized throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, therefore, including the territory of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this a decision by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and did it include the calling up of the reserve police Force or the activation of the reserve police Force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision to mobilize or to activate the reserve force or the police was taken by the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the decisions were enforced by the Ministry of the Interior, rather, the Commander within the Ministry of Interior, and so members of all three peoples were recruited, were mobilized, for the reserve police Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: About the same time, did the JNA itself become active in the Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slightly before that, the reserve police Force were mobilized. It was on 20th September 1991, we have already indicated some time towards the end of July 1991, JNA began to form its units in Serb villages, distribute weapons among them, uniforms for them, and begin to train those units in those villages. I have already indicated it, and I think it needs to be pointed out, that these units were made exclusively of members of the Serb nationalities and they were set up in villages exclusively inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any incidents involving the JNA that you yourself were involved in investigating in the Bosanski Samac area; I speak specifically of the time late November, say, from 1991 through until to, say, April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 28th November 1991 to 1st April 1992 in the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality, there were 23 subversive actions when explosive devices were used to destroy the facilities in (indecipherable) in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. These were the destruction of transmission pylons or, rather, atom bomb shelter which was in one of the enterprises in Bosanski Samac, a bridge across the Sava between Bosanski Samac and Slavonski Samac which links both Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Republic of Croatia and some other facilities. During their onset investigation by the police, some evidence was found indicating that the perpetrators of the crimes could be, could be, among the members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sort of evidence are you referring to that was relied upon to make this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because some tracks, some evidence, was found on the side, on these spots, indicating that these acts were committed by JNA people, first beginning with the explosives used for the purpose, then footprints or, rather, boot prints, boots worn by JNA men, and then the observed movements of some JNA members observed by the villagers, by local inhabitants, in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in any way interfered with in your attempt to investigate these incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean JNA, no, they did not interfere with the investigation of the facilities demolished. To begin with, they realised if they had interfered that they would show evidently that they had been perpetrators and besides they realised that there were very slight chances that the police would be able to identify the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any attempt by anyone to interfere with the police investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so. I do not think there was any interference with our work in that regard. I am referring to the onset investigation of all these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago the incident relating to the atomic shelter, I think, and the explosives used in relation to that. Do you recall when that event occurred, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, but it could have been in December 1991 or, perhaps, early 1992 -- too much time has elapsed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall an event involving a bridge across the Sava River in Bosanski Samac in early February 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that event. The bridge was demolished on 5th February '92 at 8.43. On that same, on that occasion the part of the bridge above the ground was demolished because, of course, part of the bridge spans the river itself. But the explosives placed there damaged the part which is above the ground, and then the pavement or, rather, the railway tracks that go across the bridge were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you responsible for the investigation into this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of the team which investigated the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to make any findings of who was responsible for this particular incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of information we came by, there was no dilemma that the bridge was destroyed by JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your position with the police Force, did you make any assessment as to why the JNA was involving itself in this activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my mind, there are several reasons which made the JNA commit those acts in the territory of Bosanski Samac and in the territory of some other municipalities as well. To begin with, they wanted to justify in the eyes of the citizens the presence of JNA in our territory or, rather, to create chaos, to create a chaotic situation, provoke excesses in order to create an atmosphere of insecurity among the citizens to show that the public peace and order, or law and order, were imperiled there, and the police were not able to control this situation in the territory of their municipality, and that they, therefore, JNA needed to be present in the area so as to maintain peace and order, or prevent conflicts between inhabitants or between local inhabitants. Also, some concrete activities of that kind went in pursuit of other goals, for instance, demolishing the transmission lines, I mean, the high voltage network, and thus had cut off power supply to the Republic of Croatia, and when it comes to a demolition of the bridge across the Sava, I believe that the purpose of this was to prevent Bosnian and Herzegovinan citizens who were working as migrant workers in west European countries and thus prevent them to take part in the referendum which was to take place on 28th February 1992, and was being organised by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what the purpose of this referendum was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of the referendum was to ask the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina whether they were for Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do your Honours wish to take an adjournment?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is 4 o'clock, I am sorry. (To the witness): Do you recall whilst you were in the police Force in Bosanski Samac attempts, well, a move to establish a military organisation known as the "Fourth Detachment"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, JNA began military organisation in Serb villages and appointment of commanders of detachments, rather, battalions in some of these villages. They began this activity as early as July 91. The first detachment was set up in the village of Obudovac which also had the municipal JNA command. This is the largest Serb village in the municipality of Bosanksi Samac. Another detachment was set up in Gornja Slatina, which was another Serb village. Also, I should say in early August '91, at roughly the same time, a Third Detachment in the village of Gornja Crkvina, which is also a village with a Serb population, was formed. Then some time later, I should say, in early February '92, the Fourth Detachment was formed in the town of Bosanski Samac itself. The Commander of that detachment, and I think its strength was about 500 men, its Commander became Radovan Antic, the former Secretary of SUPA Bosanksi Samac and his deputy for security was Simo Zaric, retired head of state Security Department for Bosanski Samac, (indecipherable). These are three adjacent municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric have political connections or involvement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. Could you please repeat the question? I did not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric have any involvement with politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, no, he did not have any particular political office. He was a member of the Social Democratic Party in the municipality. That was in early 1992. Before that, some time between 1974 to 1978, he was the Secretary of the Interior of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac. After that, in 1983, he was hired by the State Security Department of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is where he remained until his retirement in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the Fourth Detachment and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Fourth Detachment is a JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall at some stage a road block being set up on the road leading into Bosanski Samac? I am sorry, I will withdraw that question, your Honour. Do you recall a period of time when a number of road blocks were established in and around your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In communication access towards the town of Bosanski Samac, JNA began to set up checkpoints, I would not call them road blocks, I would rather call them checkpoints. The first such checkpoints were set in place by JNA about one kilometre out of town on the main communication access between Bosanski Samac and Orasje towards the end of '91. An identical checkpoint was set in place somewhat later on the regional road, Bosanski, Samac Gradacac, in the village of Gornja Slatina. Then some time in early March '92, the checkpoint was set up in the village, Gornja Crkvina, between Bosanski Samac and Sarajevo road, so that in this manner they could control any access, the JNA could control all the access to Bosanski Samac from all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was responsible for the control of civilian traffic in the Opstina of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Traffic control in the municipality of Bosanski Samac and all the other municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina was in the hands of the civilian police, that is, by law. So that JNA in the manner as described by setting up of those check points appropriated the right, which was very wrongful, to control civilians, the flow of goods, passenger traffic and everything else, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the JNA assisted by the Fourth Detachment in the manning and operation of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... to these checkpoints, JNA was not helping very much the Fourth Detachment. JNA practically armed, organised, supplied uniforms and everything else to the Fourth Detachment as a JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you aware, in your duties as a police Officer, of the distribution of arms to people other than the Fourth Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town itself, JNA did not distribute any weapons apart from the Fourth Detachment, by the JNA, that is only the Fourth Detachment members have received arms from the JNA. I also wish to point out, I think it is important, that the JNA distributed arms to its members, the members of other units and not only (indecipherable) but even these three former departments wrongfully, because members of these detachments usually went home. They spent the days in training and under law of Bosnia-Herzegovina citizens may not own, may not in possession of any automatic weapons. So this was a wrongful action by JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was any official explanation given for the establishment of the Fourth Detachment, I mean in terms of why was it established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in mid February 1992, the local radio station in Bosanski Samac, (indecipherable) Radovan Antic, the commander of the Fourth Detachment and Simo Zaric, his deputy for security matters, they addressed the public and gave some explanations why the Fourth Detachment had been set up as a JNA unit in the town of Bosanski Samac. On that occasion, perhaps the most important thing that needs to be pointed out, they also communicated that unit had been formed in the town in order to forestall, to prevent, interethnic conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a problem with interethnic conflict at this time which would justify the intervention of the Fourth Detachment, so far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there was no interethnic, there were no interethnic conflicts in the town itself. There was absolutely no need to set up a JNA unit in the area in order to prevent interethnic conflict in the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any incidents involving the police and the Fourth Detachment that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of the moment of the establishment of the Fourth Detachment in that town, its members and JNA used to organise patrols at night time, patrols which covered some part of the town itself. Under such circumstances, several incidents happened between JNA members and the civilian police. For instance, there was a case when three members of the Fourth Detachment fired at a police patrol in the town and, on another occasion, members of the Fourth Detachment disarmed a police patrol, civilian police patrol, which was again on its regular patrol in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any repercussions as a result of these attacks upon the police by the Fourth Detachments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the result was the anxiety of the citizens because these were the first incidents caused by JNA formation, and its citizens were quite clear that formation had no intention of doing what it was supposed to do, that is, to prevent conflict; that it was there to provoke conflict in the town, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall an organisation which had the name Commission for Exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of the moment when JNA and other formations occupied the municipality of Bosanski Samac, the larger part of its territory, the Serb side begin to establish the Commission for Exchange. That is what they called it; actually it was the Commission for ethnic cleansing of Muslims and Croats from the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was in charge of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commission had several members and in charge of it was Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said earlier in your evidence that the commander of the local JNA was Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet with him from time to time in the course of your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions I had the opportunity of talking to him about this dissolution of individual questions or, rather, attempts to solve some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic when he came to Bosanski Samac on 6th March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it on 6th March together with Captain of first class, Dragicevic -- and he was the State Security, the military intelligence officer in Brcko garrison -- the two of them came for discussion to meet us at the police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose was to discuss and to agree on the establishment of a checkpoint on the road between Dobje and Sarajevo -- Doboj and Sarajevo, sorry. I said a few moments ago that he was being accompanied by the Captain of the first rank and he was our main intelligence, rather, counter intelligence officer was accompanying him on that occasion which is Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (4.03 p.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you tell the Chamber whether this testimony that you are offering at this time relates to matters that are alleged to have occurred in the Prijedor region, or is it the purpose of this testimony to give the Chamber a picture of the overall picture of what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence is submitted for a number of reasons. Firstly, we submit it goes to the question of widespread and systematic, so that one looks beyond the Opstina of Prijedor itself to see what happened in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We will not be dealing with this sort of evidence in respect of everywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because obviously we cannot, but what will be tendered will be some evidence in relation to various area across the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina which, we will argue, at the end of the day represents a widespread or systematic attack. In addition to that, some of this evidence will go to corroborate some of the things that Dr. Gow has said, particularly in relation to the JNA and the TO and other participants in the conflict that took place in Bosnia in 1992. Further, if your Honours please, the evidence will go, we submit, to show the involvement of the Republic of Srpske and we will show, in our submission, that by this evidence the Republic of Srpske lent its facilities to this witness, in particular, which is just one small piece of evidence in relation to that. There will be evidence from this witness, your Honours, that will go to -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not think you have to tell us anything more; I think you have done pretty well already. Thank you. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Mr. Lukac, you were speaking just before the break about a meeting that you had with Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic of the JNA at your police station in March 1992. When he arrived at that particular place, was he alone or did he bring with him certain members of his particular military unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said that with him there was Captain Petrovic. He was a security officer in the barracks of the JNA at Brcko. He was an officer of the counter intelligence service of the JNA, and accompanying him was a large number of military police members that were there to secure the vehicles left in front of the police Station as well as the area in front of the police Station where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As far as your assessment of the situation at the time was concerned, was there any necessity for these military police to be present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no need for the military police to be present. As far as his personal security was concerned, he could have come alone to that meeting. What is important to say that, apart from the military police that was there to secure him while he was going to the meeting, immediately near the police Station, to be precise on the other side of the street, in a shop, there was a large number of the Fourth Detachment of the JNA from Bosanski Samac that were also there to secure Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there another incident that occurred later in March at a place called Grebnice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was at a checkpoint of the civilian police and the traffic control in the village of Grebnice. That checkpoint was on that particular day on the regional road, Bosanski Samac-Orasje. Our police patrol stopped a civilian vehicle during the night when there were two people in there, and they asked their identity papers and they showed the civilian cards, documents, but our police patrol searched the vehicle, and during that search they found two automatic pistols of the make Scorpion used solely by the JNA with silencers. During the conversation with the people who were in the vehicle and upon the question, where they were going and why they were carrying weapons, one of those said that he was a JNA major and that he was on a special mission. As he was wearing plain clothes and he did not carry a military ID, the police Officer took the weapons he found in the vehicle from them and gave them a receipt, and the next day this particular event continued. The same major, accompanied by some 20 military policemen, occupied the police Station at Bosanski Samac because he wanted the weapons to be returned to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this particular occasion, was the matter resolved by the weapons being returned to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some two weeks later the weapons that was returned to the JNA, it was returned at the barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any attempt made during this period -- I am speaking of February/March 1992 -- for the members of the reserve police to leave the police Force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In February/March 1992, members of the reserve police of Serbian nationality left the reserve police structure, and in such a way the overall position and the role of the civilian police was intended to be weakened and that was all an excuse for the presence of the JNA in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who was behind influencing these people in this way, these police officers in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my mind, the JNA was behind it, probably the security service of the JNA as well as some leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember a dispatch on 30th March 1992 being issued from Sarajevo by Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this dispatch. Momcilo Mandic was, by the way, at that time the aid to the Minister of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they sent a dispatch to all the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina in which they informed all the police officers that a Serbian SUP was created in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he indicated all the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina where there was a Serbian Ministry of Interior that was operating, and on that list was the municipality of Bosanski Samac as well. The next day after the arrival of dispatch there was another official dispatch signed by the then Minister of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Delimustafic, where it was stated that the dispatch about the creation of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior sent by Mandic was wrongful because that meant the creation of parallel police organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a meeting of the police Officers, and what was the result of the meeting of police fficers in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day a meeting was held, a meeting of all the people who worked at our police Station, and I was present at the meeting. Both dispatches were read, the one signed by Mr. Momcilo Mandic about the creation of a Serbian Ministry of Interior, and the dispatch signed by our official Minister for the Interior, Mr. Delimustafic. All the employees of the police Station unanimously declared loyalty to the legal Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that every employee except one signed personally dispatch, a list, and that list signed by a representative of the Muslim and the Croatian employees was sent to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the Serbian employees of the police Force, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the Serbian, the Serbian employees in our police station also signed their loyalty. There was just one member of the Serb employees who did not sign it and he was appointed by the Serbian Democratic Party to his post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the latter half of 1992 was there established a particular body in Bosanski Samac, a representative body, in order to deal with issues concerning the JNA the police and other governmental bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the latter part of March 1992 in the town of Bosanski Samac was formed a body where there were representatives of all the political parties in the town; the representatives of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, the representative of the police station and the representative of the Fourth Detachment of the JNA in the town. The purpose of forming of such a body was that in this new situation one should monitor the security situation in the town of Bosanski Samac itself, not in the municipality and that, in accordance with the new situation, tries to find adequate and timely solutions for problems that might appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this body meet from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This body would practically meet every day, very regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall a meeting in 13th April 1992 at which meeting the gentleman that you referred to earlier, Simic, arrived late?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting on 13th April 1992 relates not to this body but to the representatives of some political parties. That was held at the President of the municipalities of Bosanski Samac office and was organised by the Deputy President of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Present were the representatives of the three major political parties of the Serbian Democratic Party, the Croatian Democratic Union and the Party of Democratic Action, not only from the territory of municipality of Bosanski Samac, but of the municipalities of Bosanski Samac, Orasje, Modricia, Gradacac and Osijek. These were all adjacent municipalities. At the same meeting were present the Presidents of the municipalities that I have mentioned, and at the same meeting was present a representative of the JNA, a Colonel Tutavic. He was born in the area of the Bosanski Samac municipality and at that time he was working in the general headquarters of the JNA in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that meeting the President of the Serbian Democratic Party of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, Mr. Blago Simic, had practically informed all the present that the Serbian municipality of Samac was being created, and this particular municipality was first created in December 1991. For the first time in public, in the presence of these people, he described the boundaries of that municipality that was about to be formed, and that was called the municipality, the Serbian municipality of Samac and the chief town was to be Bosanski Samac. He gave as well a deadline of seven days to the representatives of the Serb, of the Muslim and Croatian nationality to decide about the proposal on the boundaries of this Serbian municipality and the actual territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any discussion at the time, questions directed to Simic about what would happen to the Croat and Muslim population in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such a question was put by the President of the Croatian Democratic Union, and the answer was that the Croatian and Muslim population on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Samac had to leave from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "leave", was there any discussion about where they would go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no particular discussion about it. He simply said the Croatian Muslim population had to move from the area. He did not say where to. That practically meant that some 10,000 Croats and Muslims from the area had to leave as if they had never previously lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 10th April 1992 were you appointed the Chief of police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 11th April 1992 upon the proposal of the Croatian Democratic Union and the Ministry of the Interior I was appointed Acting Chief of police Station in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the conditions like in the city of Bosanski Samac at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there was quite a lot of concern and anxiety among the population, taking into account a whole situation in the area of our municipality and the presence of the units of the JNA which operated on the territory of the municipality and had checkpoints in all, on all the communication axes that led to the town and in the town itself, but nevertheless there were no inter-ethnic conflicts in the town itself or on the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On or about the 12th of April, maybe a little earlier, did you in your capacity receive as an Acting Chief of police receive information from a citizen in Batkusa about an event that had occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 12th April 1992 as the Chief of police I received information from the citizens and from our civilian police patrols that in the Serbian village of Batkusa, which was in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, some 30 people in uniforms had arrived from the Republic of Serbia in that village and that unit which had infantry weapons had been transported by two helicopters of the JNA and put them in the youth centre in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you understand these people to be part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was difficult at that moment to conclude whether they belonged to the JNA or not, but the fact itself that they were transported by the JNA helicopters one could conclude that the JNA organised their arrival in that area. The uniforms they wore at that time were different from the ones that the members of the JNA wore in our area. Those were camouflage uniforms worn exclusively by some special units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever later discover who this group was, the identification of this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those conditions we had no exact information about the identity of that group, but later on I learned that these were members of a paramilitary group which most probably belonged to the extreme wing of the radical party in Serbia, the head of which is Borislav Seselj. The largest part of the members of those units that later on appeared under the name of "grave wars" came from the Republic of Serbia and mostly from the territory of the municipality of Kragujevac, that is also in Serbia. Among them there was a less important number of members that came from the territory of the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the month of April 1992 was an attempt made by the government in Sarajevo, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to reactivate the TO in the Bosanski Samac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I have described previously, the TO that had existed up until 1990 had been disactivated, as Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have its own army and, apart from the police, no official armed forces. The government and the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 6th April 1992, they decided to establish a Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. By that decision of the presidency and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina they asked all the municipality bodies to implement that decision as the JNA had previously taken the weaponry, as I have mentioned earlier. All the citizens from the municipality in Bosanski Samac and in all Bosnian municipalities, indeed, could volunteer into the Territorial Defence. It is also very important to decide what was the aim of the creation of the TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that aim was that the TO unit should be put to protect law and order in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your understanding of how this particular TO unit would work with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Taking into account the fact that the JNA or, more precisely, the Fourth Detachment of the JNA in Bosanski Samac had stated they were there in order to protect law and order, the security of the citizens, to protect the property of the citizens and to prevent national clashes, the same task was given to the TO. From that point of view, if the TO and the JNA were, had the same task and were on the same mission, it was very normal to expect that they would work on the same project, that is the protection of law and order in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the state structures, but obviously the intentions of the JNA were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the reaction to any suggestion that this TO unit would work within either the Fourth Detachment or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the meeting of the working body which was at the level of the town of Bosanski Samac, I explained previously what was in that body and what this was meant to do, that was the body that was meeting regularly every day. Well, a meeting was held on the evening of 16th April 1992, and that was two days after the implementation of the decision by the government and the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the creating of TO in Bosanski Samac. For those reasons at that meeting for the first time were present the newly appointed commander of the TO and head of the headquarters of the TO. At the same meeting was present Mr. Simo Zaric as representative of the Fourth Detachment of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this decision to create this new TO received well by the JNA or the Fourth Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That decision was not accepted by the JNA because at that particular meeting on 16th April 1992 the newly appointed commander of the TO offered to Mr. Zaric that the Fourth Detachment should become a part of the TO of Bosanski Samac, that they work together on the protection of law and order, but Mr. Zaric refused that and said that the Fourth Detachment was part of the JNA and, therefore, it could not be part of the TO; it was part of the JNA and so it could not be part of TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a consequence of this, was it necessary for your police to provide protection to the TO and their establishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police was not protecting the units of the TO because the units that had to be formed were of a military character, so they were in a position to protect themselves, but the task was that the civilian police and the formed TO units worked together on the protection of law and order on the territory of the muncipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Later I think on the same day of the 16th April did you accompany the TO commander to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I as the Chief of police of the police station I was present at that meeting at Bosanski Samac and the head of the TO was there, the representatives of the political parties, Mr. Zaric as the representative of the Fourth Detachment of the JNA. After the meeting the head of the TO who lived in a village in our muncipality asked me to accompany him with my duty vehicle because he had to go through a checkpoint, a Serbian checkpoint, in the village of Srpska Tisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to get through these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we came to the checkpoint, that checkpoint had been there for the previous several months, I noticed that at that particular checkpoint no JNA soldiers were there; nobody was there in fact, except for some iron barricades that were put there in order to slow down the traffic. So I accompanied this man and very near I noticed later on a member of the JNA who was going from the checkpoint towards the interior, the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about the way this soldier was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His detail which I had not noticed before on JNA members in our area, he was wearing the JNA uniform of the olive brown colour. As it was a raining he had a cape, a cape made of canvas to protect him against the rain as it was also blowing. As I came to meet him I saw that the wind had blown the cape over his shoulder, and I could see a white ribbon on his shoulder tied to the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know the significance of this white ribbon when you first saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know what it was supposed to signify, but such white ribbons tied on the shoulders of the JNA members I had seen on television before as we watched them taking Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then make any enquiries about the presence of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 300 metres behind that soldier I saw another soldier. He was also wearing a white ribbon on his shoulder and it all intrigued me, that is I wanted to learn the reason why they were wearing those white ribbons tied in that particular way. Around 10 p.m. that evening I came to the police station and there intended to ask the policemen on duty in the police station, I wanted to check the information about the security situation in the territory of the muncipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you told? What did you discover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told this policeman about the soldier with a white ribbon that I had seen, and he then called Simo Zaric of the JNA Fourth Detachment in the town, we wanted to learn what were the reason for those white ribbons worn on their uniforms. So, Mr. Zaric then in the telephone conversation said that he did not know the reason for those ribbons worn by the soldiers and that he would try to come by some information to learn what it was all about. During that evening, within about an hour or so, he called us again and told us that he had tried to learn something about this and that it was a JNA unit set up in the village of Srpska Tisina, that they were going to have a drill that night, that they were wearing those so they could recognise each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you ever seen JNA personnel ever wearing uniforms with this type of white ribbon that you speak of before on a previous occasion, other than what you have seen on television in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I have not seen them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you had made these enquiries, did you go back to your home that night and what happened during the course of the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime around 2.25 on 17th April 1992 the town resounded with fire from automatic weapons. I wanted to see what was happening and I tried to call by telephone the person on duty in the police station from my flat, but I realised that the telephones had been cut off. That night practically JNA, JNA members and this paramilitary group from Serbia which had arrived on the 11th April to Batkusa that night they took Bosanski Samac, the town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do when this happened, when the town was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that halted attempt to telephone, because, as I have said, the lines had been cut off, I noticed that from a building in a neighbouring street a fire was open towards the building in which I had my flat fired from sniper weapons. So that I realised that I was covered in that building, in that residential building, and that it would not come out. As I was alone in the flat, I moved to my neighbour's flat, who is a Muslim by the way, and I stayed there until the morning when the telephone lines began to function again which was about 5 o'clock. Then I called again the policeman on duty in the police station, but in spite of repeated calls nobody answered several of the numbers that I tried to dial, and it was clear to me that the police station had been taken by those forces. Other neighbours also let us know that a city had been occupied, and that members in camouflage uniforms with some specific insignia which were radicals because they were wearing some white brimmed camouflage hats and some something like that; they were searching the town and controlling some of the vital facilities, so that is the radio station, the police station and the post office, access bridges to the town, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then decide to try to escape from the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came by a complete information and learned that the town had been occupied by the JNA, I realised they would come to arrest me and I tried to leave the town. I tried to do it in a certain way and I partly succeeded to get out of the town itself, but then the road that I had taken was blocked by JNA members, and in the village of Gornja Crkvina I came across a road block put up by JNA members. There they stopped me and practically arrested me, on 10th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then hand to this person that stopped you your identification documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were intercepted by a policeman, that is a man wearing a police uniform. On his head he wore a beret with a Serbian tricolour flag. I say this because this was the first time that I saw the flag, tricolour flag, on a helmet. He asked for my ID. I gave him my driving licence. He read it and he read my first name and my surname. He said: "You're the one", and he immediately ordered me to get off the vehicle in this village in front of the, in the yard, and after that we were searched and detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was detained in that village for three days. This was the office of the local office, and during those three days there were 10 to 15 persons detained. They were mostly citizens whose identification was checked on that road and who were then taken into custody and detained in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after being kept there for three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Sunday which, was 19th April 1992, five of us detained there were put on a truck guarded by five members of the police and army, and they took us to Bosanski Samac to the town. When we arrived in Bosanski Samac the truck stopped in front of the gate to the former military defence facility; that building and these facilities are across the street from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you taken inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they took us into the yard of that building and there I observed that in front of the metal door that was the warehouse until 1990, the Territorial Defence weaponry was kept there, in front of that door there were two policemen standing on guard. They opened that door. They took us into that depot, into that storage space. When we entered I saw that there were between 30 to 50 men detained there. Those were men I knew, that is I had been seeing them around the town, around Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was were the nationality of the men that you knew that you saw that were being kept as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened while you were there being held in detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I came those men were sitting with their backs towards the walls in that storage room, and they had blankets over their knees, they were sitting there. Could I see that some of them had injuries on their faces and I could, therefore, infer that they had been ill-treated. There were also some of my policemen among them who had spent the night on duty and were detained that night. So that we were accommodated there together with them. A year or two later, after we had arrived that metal door of that storage room opened and a man whom I did not know entered, he was wearing a camouflage uniform and he came to the centre of the room, to the middle of the room, and he was holding a police truncheon in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The translation that you have here is "a year or two later". It was not a year or two later; I take it that it was sometime later, about an hour later, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he entered the room what happened? When this person entered the room what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When this individual entered the storage room I noted that all the men who had already been there, who were under detention there, they put down their heads and they were looking at the concrete, at the floor, and I noticed that fears, I could sense fear in that room when he entered that room. I concluded, therefore, that this was not the first time that he had entered that room, and that he was, roughly speaking, that he had some kind of power over the men detained in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say when he entered the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he entered he asked who was new among the detainees. So, everybody was silent, nobody said anything, so he repeated the question. I realised then that the five of us who had just arrived were the new ones, the newcomers, that he meant us. Then I stood up and I said I was new there, and he ordered me to come close to him and stand before him and I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when you stood before him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me then my name. I told him and he asked me what I was doing before I was arrested, and I told him that I was the head of the police station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he then say something to you -- sorry, did he then do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that very moment he hit me with his police baton he had in his right hand, and they (indecipherable) on the left hand side, on my left side, and he repeated the blow on severa occasions and then he hit me with his boot in the stomach, so I gasped, lost my breath and I fell on the concrete. Then I heard, I was semi-conscious, and he told me "Get up Bre".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What do you understand about the word Bre, B-R-E?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a bi-word which is used in Serbia only in the dialect which is the Ekaski dialect in Serbia. I, therefore, concluded that he had come from Serbia and that he was a member of that paramilitary unit who arrived in the territory of our muncipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a mechanical aid I got up, I stood up when he ordered me and he beat me again, so I fell and he beat me again. The total lasted about some 10 minutes, after which he stopped, he left, went out and closed the door of that storage room. After that other detainees came to help me and I asked them who was the man, and they told me that he was the person called Lugar which is a nickname which is common in our country, in our part of the country. Then subsequently I learnt also the identity of that person. His name was Slobodan Milakovic and he comes from Kragujevac, that is from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now on the next day, this is 20th April, were you then taken out of that building to another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day policemen came. They took me out from the storage room and they took me to the building of the police across the street from that facility where we were detained. Then they took me to an office in that police station and there I found a large number of persons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to determine where these people had come from, which organisations and so forth they had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four persons were in that office, Stefan Dadorovic, a man who after the occupation of Bosanski Samac by Serb authorities was appointed the head of the Serb police. The second one was Milan Jekic, a former police commander before he resigned prior to the events. The third person was security officer who worked in the command with Lieutenant Colonel Stephen Nikolic of the 17th Operational Technical Group, but he was in civilian clothes and a leather jacket. The fourth person I did not know. It was a plan of about 50 years of age with a long grey beard, in a camouflage uniform. He was sitting in a chair and on his knees he had a rifle, a pumparica rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then interrogated about the existence of a radio station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated by Stefan Dadorovic, the newly appointed head of police. He asked me for a registration which I did not have and he insisted on my telling where that radio station was and I tried to explain to him that I did not have any registration, that outside the police station I had absolutely no registration or did I have anything like that in my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now some 30 to 60 minutes later did a group of men dressed in military uniform enter the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that interview I was taken back to the storage room in the Territorial Defence, and I joined other people who were there. Then about an hour later after the interview that storage room was entered by a group of persons in camouflage uniform. I would not know how many of them there were, six, seven, up to 10 ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- entered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what particular military unit these men belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They belonged to the paramilitary formation Serbia, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they do when they came in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They ordered a number of detainees to come out into the yard, I think three or four of them and I was among them. So we came out into the yard in front of this storage room, the yard has concrete pavement, and they immediately began to beat us, two or three of them would pick out one of us and start physical, with physically harassing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this treatment of you continue over the period of the next few days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such procedure went on the last days throughout that week. It was a Monday, so daily, day in and day out, sometimes several times a day, but it was more or less an identical way. They would take out men into that yard and physically harassing them, hitting them beating them, dealing them blows with anything that was at their disposal, with rifle butts, boots, metal pipes and various other objects that they probably found around the yard. Then on third or fourth day of that week when they entered they started asking us to sing them Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you badly injured during the course of this period yourself by the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that repeated or rather daily ill-treatment I was in a rather bad state; my skull was fractured; I lost several teeth; I was battered and beaten all over. So that my health was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the conditions like in the camp, can you give us a description of the conditions in terms of the food and the hygiene and so forth that you experienced there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that room the conditions were very bad. It was the room of about 12 metres long, about 6 to 7 metres wide. There were 50 of us in it. We slept on the concrete. There was nothing, there were no mattresses or anything. There were a couple of those army blankets that they had thrown in at the beginning, and they brought us food there, breakfast and supper and for lunch they used to put us on a truck and take us to an enterprise and there in a canteen they provided us with meals. So the sanitation conditions were very bad. They would allow the prisoners to go to the washroom in the next building once or twice a day. The conditions, the facilities were such that it is difficult to describe it to persons who have not experienced anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall on or about 26th April at about 5 o'clock in the afternoon hearing a shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 5.30, 1730 that afternoon we heard, a pistol shot. The bullet penetrated this metal door, the metal plate on the door and hit the wall. It was fired roughly at the height, the chest height of a man in a standing position. After that the door of the storage room opened, and the person called Lugar, Slobodan Milakovic, entered. I remembered well he was wearing a white sweat suit and under his armpit he had the pistol in a case and in a hand he had a wooden stick of about a metre and a half long, and as he entered he began to strike prisoners who were by the wall, by the right-hand wall from the door. His blows were very hard and he struck them in the head. Whenever he would indulge in such bloody orgies that was what he did. He hit several times with that stick and a man who was the fourth or fifth in that row, Branic Anto, and this is a man who is in his 50s and in rather poor health or rather poor physique, and he therefore fell on the floor in a coma and he continued to deal him blows in the head several times till the man was semi-dead. Then he ordered two detainees to take him out and put him in front of the door of the storage room which they did and then he took out the pistol from the case and fired two bullets in the back of his head because the man was lying face to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Later on that evening at approximately 10.30 did you hear trucks coming into the yard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That same evening around 22.30 we heard how army trucks entered the yard in front of the building where we were, and after a short while the door to the storage room opened and some five or six military policemen entered. They had those white belts that military police usually are distinguished by. They were JNA military policemen. After that several Serb policemen arrived and then they explained that they would read a list of persons and the persons whose names would be read out should board those parked trucks, the trucks parked right in front of the door of the storage room. Then they read out the lists and the majority of those present were read out so that we were put on those trucks. I remember there were 47 of us. Four persons remain in the storage room they were not on that list. One of them asked why their names had not been called out and why they were not being boarded on to that truck, and they were answered they would stay there and would be used for exchange. Then we drove away and I should like to emphasise that of those four persons who stayed behind two were killed some time later, that is on 7th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The trucks that drove you away, were they JNA trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were two JNA trucks covered with canvas, and before and after those trucks there was the military police of the JNA that accompanied them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go in the trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those trucks took us to the JNA barrack at Brcko. Upon our arrival we were searched in a hall at the entrance of the prison buildings and then after that our hands were tied by rope behind our backs, each person individually. After that we were put in the cells that were in that military prisons at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anything happen during the course of that first night that you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing more significant happened during that first night, but the next day in the cell where I was with other two people came Mr. Simo Zaric who was the deputy of the commander of the Fourth Detachment from Bosanski Samac in charge of the security. He was wearing a camouflage uniform and on his left epaulette he had a white ribbon tied on it as the soldiers were wearing during the attack on Bosanski Samac. Accompanying him was the prison manager whose name I do not know, as well as Captain Petrovic, the security officers, officer of the JNA in those barracks. I asked Mr. Zaric then why we were held there; it has been 10 days when we, since we have been in prison and abused and nobody gave us any explanation why we were there, no any court proceedings were taken against us in case we were guilty of anything. He answered then that the six of us had the status of political prisoners and we were going to stay on until further notice. Then he gave me the names of the persons who had the same status as myself and I was on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you observe who was around at about this camp in terms of the personnel that were guarding while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That camp, that is that prison was in the jurisdiction of the JNA, and military police were guarding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 30th April 1992 during the course of the night did you hear an explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Very early in the morning, I cannot remember the exact time, but I could hear a very strong explosion and the paint from the ceiling of the frame in the prison where we fell down. So we were aware that something had happened in the town, that some of the objects was mined. Later on we learned that the bridge over the River Sava at Brcko was destroyed, the one that links Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a question, Mr. Niemann, if I may about the time that you expect that you will need for the presentation of the Prosecution's direct case. I have reviewed the list of witnesses that you will call and, looking at the maximum time that you have indicated for those witnesses, my calculation, well, actually it is my secretary's calculation, will be 17 weeks and minimum -- well, the maximum of the "will call" would be 17 weeks; the maximum of the "may call" is 7.5. That is a total of 24.5 weeks, that is about six months. When we met in March I believe you had indicated six to nine weeks. First of all, the reason I mentioned before we began this afternoon is that I wanted you to check my math.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that terribly off? Is it so far off? 24.5 weeks is your estimate for a maximum of "will call" and "may call". A minimum of "will call" and "may call" is 15.5 weeks, that is about four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I think, your Honour, when we first did our calculation there were a couple of matters that we did not consider, and that was, we did not consider that we would only be sitting for four days. I think our original calculation was for a five-day week. We also had hoped to be able to proceed through the witnesses at a fairly speedy rate, but we had no idea at the time just how long cross-examination was going to be. It is very hard.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This estimate does not include cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am aware of that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, your Honour, except that some of the witnesses we are calling in the early part of the case where the time is longer, are witnesses who will take longer to testify, because they are dealing with ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If it is going to take a moment I suppose we can dismiss the witness, if that is acceptable with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it for this evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukac, you are excused for the evening. You should return back tomorrow at 2.30. We will not begin until 2.30, Mr. Niemann and Mr. Orie, because this Trial Chamber has another matter to consider in the morning and, as you understand, we have one courtroom and you are in it. So we have another matter that we have to handle in the morning. I apologise. So, Mr. Lukac, we will continue with your testimony tomorrow at 2.30 p.m. You are excused. You may leave. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have made a very detailed assessment of the Prosecution case in terms of what we believe we require in order to prove the case. Obviously, if down the road we receive indications or something that parts of the case are admitted or that there are stipulations in relation to any of it, that could have a substantial effect on the amount of evidence we have to call. But this is our best assessment based on having to prove the case and carrying the burden which we need to do. I mean we have endeavoured as much as possible to ensure that every piece of the evidence is essential for our case. Now, no doubt there may be from time to time pieces of evidence which may not be absolutely necessary for that purpose. I cannot vouch for being so precise as not to call evidence that is, in some way, viewed as a repetition, but most of it, your Honour, is designed to that end. It is a big case in that sense and it covers a wide perspective. It is to be distinguished, I think, from the ordinary sort of domestic case that we encounter because of the extra burdens that are imposed upon the Prosecution in terms of the international nature of the offence and the widespread or systematic nature of the crimes that have to be proved, and the fact that it is the very first case that we have presented. For all those reasons, it is proving to be a bigger task than we had hoped it would be. But in order to answer your Honour, yes, it may take as long as what your Honour said, but we will use every endeavour to try to ensure that it does not and we will use every endeavour to try to reduce the length of time that the witnesses are in the box, by using such means, if we do not receive objections from the Defence, to try to lead them through parts of the evidence which otherwise might slow down the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, I certainly did not mean to cut you off. At this point I suppose I was hoping that our math was off, but I see it is not. So, we are looking at a possibility if it is maximum of "will call" and "may call", we are looking at six months.
